description: This is a five-movement suite that utilizes neoclassical elements of structure, form and compositional techniques combined with an avant-garde harmonic language and extended techniques. The main compositional techniques used throughout are ostinato, canon, and a line played by trading notes between instruments. The first movement “Andante ma non troppo” opens with a quarter and half note ostinato on E in the left hand of the piano. The bassoon and flute enter in canon on a four eighth note tied to a long note motif. The right hand of the piano joins in and turns it into six notes in a row. Next, a new motif consisting of a dotted eighth, sixteenth followed by two eighths and a quarter note tied to a long note is presented in a canon. Eventually, a return of the original material occurs with an arpeggiated ostinato in the piano instead. The next movement “Adagio” features a tremolo in the piano, a disjunct half note line in the bassoon and a melody in the flute consisting of staccato sixteenth followed by a rest on each beat. Next, a contrasting allegro section with an eighth note motif occurs in a canon in the winds overtop of an E♭ major arpeggio ostinato in the piano. Halfway through the section the arpeggio becomes polytonal with D major in the right hand and F# major in the left hand. A return to the opening section occurs with slight variations such as the bassoon line is descending now and the flute has quarter notes. This is followed by another allegro section with similar material but in different polytonalities such as C major and D major simultaneously. The next movement has no title or tempo description besides half note equals 100. It consists of either ostinato passages or chords in the piano underneath alternating sections of polyphony and trading notes in the winds consisting of quarter, eighth and sixteenth notes. The movement concludes with a long note that becomes air noises in the winds. The fourth movement “Andante” mainly consists of a cluster chord in the piano which the flute plays a solo overtop of. Eventually, the bassoon enters in dialogue playing a variation of the line. The final movement “Allegro” consists of alternating sections of polyphony often in a trading texture between the winds and homorhythmic overtop of accompaniment figures in the piano. This climaxes into a four measure multiphonic in the winds overtop of sixteenth note ostinato in the piano to conclude the piece.

key: I (C major), II (D major), III (F major)
description: This is a three-movement work that incorporates elements of folk song and dance into neoclassical structures. The first movement “Allegretto '' opens with an ostianto of dissonant articulated eighth notes in the upper winds. The bassoon enters with an energetic folk-like melody. This develops into the ostinato becoming consonant in the horn and clarinet while the oboe has an arpeggiated sixteenth note passage. This leads into a “piu mosso” section which contrasts the opening with a lyrical melody in the horn, a drone on B in the bassoon, and accompaniment figures in the oboe and clarinet. This develops into a homorhythmic passage in the ensemble to wind down into a short three note horn solo. A return to the opening character occurs with variations and fragmentation of the earlier material. After a silence, a final grave in a chorale style ends the movement. The next movement “Moderato con moto” is in ternary form. The first section features a folk-like melody first in the flute then the oboe overtop of accompaniment tenuto quarter notes in the rest of the ensemble. The next section “marcato” has an accented ostinato on the pitch D combined with an accented melody in the rest of the ensemble. The opening material returns with some variations such as the flute and oboe playing the melody at the same time in octaves and a countermelody added in the clarinet. The final movement “Moderato” opens with a canon-like entrance on long tones in the ensemble with a melody in the flute. The next section “marciale” features a dance-like section consisting of a dotted eighth and sixteenth followed by two eighth notes ostinato in horn and clarinet, arpeggiated sixteenths in the flute with occasional interjections from the oboe and bassoon. This develops into the whole ensemble playing a staccato sixteenth passage. Finally, earlier material returns leading conclude the piece

description: This is a short one-movement work in ternary form that highlights the technical and articulation capabilities of the bassoon. It opens with an “allegro molto” section with a two measures piano introduction that introduces a two-measure motif based on a dotted eighth, sixteenth, eighth in an upper neighbour motion that comes back throughout. The bassoon enters with a pickup to the third measure with the first theme that is eighth notes in a staccato arpeggiated manner outlining e minor that ends in scalar sixteenths. The piano plays a countermelody in the right hand and chords in the left-hand underneath. This continues developing with slight texture changes in the piano until a “meno mosso” section, where the opening piano motif returns combined with a more lyrical and slurred melody in the lower register of the bassoon. This is interrupted by a short “Poco piu mosso” section that is similar to the opening but introduces articulated sixteenths in the bassoon line. Next, a return to the meno mosso occurs. This develops with the opening piano motif occurring in the bassoon, which leads into an accelerando taking the music back to the original tempo and opening material. This continues with some slight variations until a final and short five measure “Vivo” section to conclude the piece in a fiery and energetic character.

description: This is a one-movement work with various short sections that are attacca each exploring a different character while employing a variety of extended techniques. The piece combines elements of traditional sound production and harsher, unconventional modern techniques and aesthetics. The opening section “Distant light from the depth” consists of a single repeated note motif that begins as one long tone with rests and evolves overtime to become more rhythmic. Over time various extended techniques and audible exhaling and inhaling from the musicians is incorporated into the texture. This leads into “Windy” that incorporates air noises with small fragments and the one note motif that is now transformed into a note that glissandos stepwise alternating around the ensemble. The next section “Soft and vicious” returns to a thinner texture and calmer character consisting of long tones throughout the ensemble. In the next section “Annoying” the glissando motif is rhythmically shortened and repeated in closer succession to create a more joking character. Then “With gloomy obsession” returns to the previous character and motifs. Next, “Leggierio” utilizes the technique quasi ricochet to create a busy and active texture that allows the piece to climax into an “Like an improvisation” that is a contrapuntal-like texture with multiple motifs that are interacting in a cohesive manner. This then returns to another “With gloomy obsession” section. Next, “Anxious fatality” utilizes extended techniques to develop the single note motif. This develops into “Crystals” where we get a section similar to the opening but with more dissonance. The rest of the piece continues to expand upon the motifs established by different combinations of extended techniques, instrumentation, and combination of motifs to explore the various textures that an ensemble can produce through three main sections: “Interludio I”, “Hidden light”, and “Interludio II”. The final section creates the most active and busiest texture that climaxes with musicians grabbing and throwing a book. Overall, the piece experiments with how a single note can be developed in an ensemble through a variety of short character changes.

description: This is a one-movement work with various short sections that are attacca each with a different character while exploring a variety of extended techniques. The opening section “Annoying but resolute” has an ironic and joking character achieved through a two sixteenth with a large interval jump to an eighth note motif combined with lots of accented notes, grace notes and glissandos. The second section “Pompous, majestic” has a quirky character through constant trading of staccato triplet sixteenths throughout the ensemble in a changing pattern through metered changes and accents. Next, “Shrilly and boring” consists of a short motif that is looped that accelerandos in a short section “Desperately” which sequences the motif higher before arriving at “Dramatically.” This features three disjunct lines based on large intervals that are weaving in and out of one another. Eventually, the parts come together and interact in a call and response manner that gradually becomes one cohesive idea. The next section “Like a bird” is a homorhythmic section with short interjections utilizing extended techniques such as quartertones and frullato imitating a bird call. This is followed by “like an improvisation” which alternates between thick contrapuntal lines and homorhythmic passages featuring the use of trills and vibrato. The next section “Broken organ” is another homorhythmic passage that slowly unravels and becomes more dissonant imitating a machine breaking apart. Then “Love song” occurs which is an oboe solo overtop of long tones in the clarinet and bassoon that explore the concept of pitch by switching between various extended techniques to change the pitch and timbre. This leads into the final section “Love song from the depths” which features a melodic line in the oboe with an intertwined accompaniment of sixteenths in the bassoon and sextuplets in the clarinet with rests interspersed throughout.

description: This is a one-movement work based on a theme from Dmitri Shostakovich’s opera Lady Macbeth (1934) and was renamed Katerina Izmailova. This opera ideologically highlighted the corruption created by Marxism in the Soviet Union depicting characters imprisoned by their circumstances. This was a reflection of how Soviet society trapped the average citizen to blindly obey the rules and protocols of the regime, creating a difficult environment to live in. Musically, the opera had Western inspiration from Alban Berg’s opera Wozzeck through the use of integral interludes and passacaglia-based forms as opposed to separate arias and choruses, typical in Russian operas. Komlikova’s piece explores the different characters such as legato vocal-like lines and humoresque staccato passages that the bassoon can achieve through six variations that follow the story of the opera. The opening of the piece, “Epigraph '' presents an introduction solo in the bassoon. Then, for the theme the piano joins in an accompaniment role, mostly providing bass line. The first variation “Rigidly” is a declamatory call and response between the bassoon and the piano. The next variation “Clouding of the mind” opens with a string of eighth notes in the bassoon, which the piano takes over turning it into an accompaniment role while the bassoon presents an elongated version of the theme. The third movement “An unstoppable impulse” is in a quicker tempo utilizing a quarter note followed by an eighth note combined with a string of eighth notes to climax to high Eb in the bassoon that is held for a long time while the piano unwinds into the next variation “Heartfelt.” This variation is a long legato line in a vocal quality in the bassoon with short interjections in the piano. This leads to a quasi-cadenza moment in the bassoon. The fifth movement “Ironically” is typical staccato and humoresque bassoon writing featuring articulated scalar passages and large interval jumps. The final variation “Com improvvisato” is a quasi-improvised section where the bassoon and piano are in dialogue with one another never playing at the same time. This leads into a final “Coda” section is a still and sparse section depicting Katerina’s suicide with only the cold water keeping her story alive. The bassoon mainly plays long notes and short fragments of the original motif while the piano plays open chords in the left-hand and the original motif in the right hand. This texture slowly dies away into just the bassoon blowing air into the instrument with no reed representing the end of her life fading away.

description: This is a five-movement suite taking inspiration from folklorism through the depiction of the average village life combined with romantic structures and harmonies. The first movement “Morning in the Garden” is marked in an Allegro vivace tempo in an ABA Coda form. It features two motifs that quickly pass around the ensemble. In the A section a motif of four sixteenth notes and an eighth note - ascending perfect fourth followed by descending stepwise motion. In the B section a motif of two sixteenths and two eighths - ascending stepwise motion ending with a descending minor third. The next movement “Melody” marked Andante cantabile is in a polyphonic texture presenting a melody in the oboe, countermelody in the clarinet, and a bass line ostinato in the bassoon. The flute switches around their role throughout between melody and bass line. The following movement “Pastoral” marked Andantino that consists of a melody that passes around the ensemble overtop of long tones. The fourth movement “Humoresque” marked Allegro non troppo is an AABA Coda form. The A section has a joking character through the use of staccato eighths and accented quarter notes. The B section marked Un poco piu mosso has two main sections: 1) virtuosic passage of sixteenth notes overtop of a countermelody and a bass line and 2) an eighth note bass line in the bassoon underneath a syncopated eighth note motif in the flute and oboe. Eventually, the B section unwinds becoming a fragmented one beat motif that leads into a fermata chord to set up a reprise of the A material. The final movement “Raining” is in ternary form. The A section marked Allegro scherzando (quasi presto) has a frantic character features a quarter note section where the ensemble is chasing the flute. The ensemble plays on the downbeat while the flute plays on beats two and three. The flute line develops into eighth notes as the phrase progresses. The B section marked Un poco meno mosso is in a cantabile and lyrical style presenting a folk-like melody in the oboe over a dotted half note accompaniment. Then a leggiero melody is presented in the clarinet overtop of a quarter rest followed by two quarter notes accompaniment. A return to the first melody occurs this time in the flute and bassoon.

description: This is a one-movement work that the title takes inspiration from the ancient architectural monument Akkerman Fortress in Odesa dating back to the thirteenth-century that has a rich history of withstanding many sieges and attacks from other various forces. The work begins with a motif of two sixteenths leading to four repeated eighth note in the bassoon. The rest of the ensemble responds to this with fragmentation, while the bassoon slowly develops this motif. As each instrument's fragment or motif expands into ostinato figures it creates a contrapuntal texture with the lines weaving in and out of one another. After the material climaxes the bass clarinet and clarinet trade off a one-measure melodic fragment that leads to a whole note with each successive fragment undergoing a ritardando to set up the next section. This section begins with longer note values that are changing independently in their own pattern in each instrument. The use of frullato is introduced into the texture to explore the different timbres possible throughout the ensemble. A quarter note theme that dynamically swells emerges from this texture in a perfect fifth interval in the alto saxophone and bass clarinet. This develops by the clarinet joining into this theme, while the longer note value texture disappears allowing room for an arpeggiated bass line to take over in the bassoon. As the section is climaxing the bassoon’s bass line rhythmic diminution becomes sixteenth notes to create more energy that leads into a trilled fermata dissonant chord that dies away. The next section is homorhythmic in a more march-like character achieved through either dotted or triplet sixteenth note rhythms. This texture is interrupted by virtuosic cadenza moments by the clarinet. Afterwards, the alto saxophone plays a new theme that incorporates motifs from the march-like section that prompts a contrapuntal treatment of this theme and its fragments in the ensemble before being interrupted by the original homorhytmic march and virtuosic clarinet line. The next section consists of disjunct articulated sixteenth notes that pass around the ensemble creating a interwoven texture. Eventually, the quarter note melody from earlier returns prompting a synthesis of different material and fragmentations from throughout the work to be recombined together creating new textures. This leads into a final brief four-measure chorale-like phrase of half notes that undergoes a ritardando allowing for an accented motif from earlier in homorhythm to surprise the listener to conclude the work.
Kouzan’s music is influenced by Ukrainian folk music and the composers Bartók, Schoenberg, and Varèse.
Kovaleva’s music is inspired by a turn to realism by reflecting on life through the traditions of classicism and romanticism. There is often use of folklore primary sources.

description: This is a one-movement concerto that explores a numerical system throughout the work centered around the year it was written 1991. First then is one bassoonist and nine cellists performing. The structure of the piece is based off the length it takes to pronounce the year. The work is broken down into four main sections that get shorter as it goes based off “One-Thousand”, “Nine-hundred”, “Ninety”, and “One”. Also, there are two main musical material that differ based on if the section begins with either a “1” or a “9”. The 1 sections are characterized by effective drama, sharp increases and decrease, recitative quality, dissonance, richness of tone. There is a contrast between unison and abrupt chords in a monorhythmic texture in the cellos. The bassoon participates in this by beginning and ending the work on a repetitive pitch “C#”. The nine sections are characterized by a lyrical and contemplative character with soft dynamic and timbre expressed through a flexibility of metric organization that is constantly changing. Compared to the 1 section that is mainly in 4/4. The work switches between fast and slow sections as well to create more of a contrast between the sections of the work. The writing for the bassoon is often virtuosic and in a quasi-cadenza manner. There is an exploration of the possible timbral qualities available to the bassoon. This is demonstrated through the graphic notation and directions for how much reed, how much lip pressure or amount of lip versus teeth, and different aspects of vibrato to be playing with, requiring the player to have a great control for subtle changes on the instrument. description: This is a one-movement work based on a Ukrainian folk song with five variations. Kozytsky’s music follows in the footsteps of Lysenko and other composers who incorporated folk music and nationalistic elements into their music at the end of the nineteenth century. The work opens with a forte drone on C that decrescendos for the bassoon to enter and presents the theme in the tenor register in an andante maestoso tempo. As the melody proceeds the drone chromatically descends until it arrives back at C. The first variation “Piu mosso” opens with the piano playing theme in unison, which leads into a scalar eighth note passage finally receiving harmonization. The bassoon then enters and plays the theme an octave lower than earlier overtop of chords in the piano. The next variation “Allegretto” puts the melody back in the tenor register but ornaments the majority of the notes with a trill, while the piano plays a string of chordal eighth notes. The third variation “Allegro grazioso” switches into f minor and is built on repeated staccato sixteenth notes with a typical piano accompaniment of bass line and offbeats. There is an interlude where the piano takes over the melody with the bassoon briefly playing the melody in minor in the lowest register before returning to the sixteenth motif. The following variation “Andante molto” returns to major tonality with a cantabile line where the melody starts as a pickup rather than on the beat as originally presented. This is overtop of a triplet arpeggiated piano accompaniment. Eventually, a lengthy and virtuosic bassoon cadenza emerges. It features arpeggiated and weaving sixteenth notes that leads to a disjunct eighth note line with grace notes before the upper notes and mordent on the lower notes. A short piano interlude leads into the final variation “Allegro grazioso” in a dance-like character with lively passages of articulated sixteenth notes. The variation continues developing into a poco stringendo to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work depicting the village Eschelbronn in Germany. The bassoon soloist represents Paul and the flute soloist Manuela, who were the owners of the home that the composer and his wife stayed at. The music is non-programmatic and attempts to convey the warmth the composer felt in the village as a means to express his deep gratitude to the residents' hospitality. The bassoon is the prominent voice the entire time with the flute joining in contrapuntal texture with a counter-melody. Very rarely does the play as the primary soloist, only on occasion on a short rest in the bassoon. The string orchestra and piano play accompaniment figures the entire time, often chords or short fragments in response to the soloists. The orchestra provides lush and thick harmonies for the soloist to play overtop of. Overall, the work portrays a nostalgic character.

description: This is a six-movement suite with no intended order or combination of movements. However, the composer suggests that a good mix of slow and fast movements is ideal. There is also the option to perform the work spatially with the clarinet on stage because they control the flow of the piece, and the other performers distributed around the hall with them ideally hidden from view. At the very end they should come onto the stage. Each of the movements were written separately over a twenty-year period without the titles they now have for various purposes. The titles were added once all of them were completed, revised, and combined together for The Aeolian Winds in 1993. The titles are inspired by American writer Ambrose Bierce’s “The Devil’s Dictionary” which is a satirical dictionary with common words accompanied with a humorous or satirical definition. Therefore, the titles of the movements give clues and insight about the interpretation of each movement’s character and the role they play within the suite and ensemble. “The "Dictator" is the clarinet, who initially inspires his people into action, then stomps them into the ground when they grow too independent. Who is the "Idiot.," the clarinet or the bassoon? The "Cynic" is mocking and angular. The clarinet finds himself "Alone" as his companions, the horn and the bassoon, drift away into the meaninglessness of the universe - he eventually leads the whole group to his point of view, but reality drifts back to equilibrium. "Eulogy" is a strange lament. "Reality" is illusory and elastic, rhythmically unpredictable.”53 Musically “Dictator” is in an allegro tempo and features a prominent clarinet line mainly consisting of sixteenth notes overtop of accompaniment figures in the ensemble derived from the clarinet’s opening rhythmic motif. Eventually, it leads into an aleatoric section combining the different motifs from throughout the movement. This then returns to the original texture. The “Idiot” is in a molto moderato tempo and features an improvisatory-like line in the clarinet overtop of rhythmic accompaniment. As it develops the ensemble fragments the clarinet line in a dialogue-like texture. The “Cynic” is in an allegro tempo presents a theme consisting of large intervals in the oboe with accented interruptions from the ensemble. The flute then presents a more compact theme while the accompaniment is now occurring simultaneously underneath. The movement continues with different variations and fragmentations in a contrapuntal texture before returning to material similar to the opening. “Alone” is in an andante tempo consisting of a weaving chromatic eighth note line in the flute and oboe that becomes more syncopated with the introduction of sixteenth notes and ties. Eventually, the entire ensemble joins in on this in a canon-like texture switching from their original accompaniment texture. “Eulogy” is in an adagio tempo consisting of legato and slurred figures in the flute in contrast to “strange” syncopated and accented figures in the horn. This is often overtop of chordal-like textures of half notes in the ensemble with moments of dialogue. “Reality” is in an allegro moderato tempo is mostly homorhythmic in texture with brief moments of fragments that pass around the ensemble. The motifs contrast between virtuosic passages of sixteenth notes and more chorale-like quarter note triplets.

recordings: Radio: 1) Premiere: National Public Radio System of the US as part of recital of Canadian music YouTube: 1) Matthew Nickel (bsn), Mariah Mlynarek (pno) (https://youtu.be/JfhhD4O4Zpg?si=pnTDXKxX_-tOhI8w)
description: This is a three-movement work structured in a neoclassical fashion with influence and aesthetics borrowed from modernist such as its approaches to atonality, dissonance, and textures. The first two movements of the work are in typical sonata-allegro form consisting of all of the regular elements of two themes, development, and recapitulation. The final movement is structured as a cadenza with an epilogue to conclude the work. The character of the music contrasts between two main characters: 1) restrained and lyrical and 2) agitated and rhythmically driven. The ostinato plays an important role throughout to musically bridge elements together. The harmonic language combines a wide array of influences from diatonic, chromatic, and atonal moments. The bassoon and piano play an equal role throughout the work with critical solo moments that emerge from the texture in the bassoon. The first movement “Pensive” often features flourishing arpeggiation or chordal passages in the piano while the bassoon plays a more vocal-like line. As it develops the bassoon line becomes more active becoming sixteenth duple and triplet notes. Throughout there are changing metres creating a rhythmic instability. The second movement “Agitated” contains a more dialogue-like texture with sixteenth note motifs passing between the bassoon and the right hand of the piano overtop of a sixteenth note oscillating ostinato motif. Often the passing dialogue will begin on a syncopation on the second sixteenth in the bassoon rather than perfectly lining up on the beat to take over. Eventually, the ostinato unwinds to an eighth note motif to allow a change to the more restrained and lyrical character. However, the intervals are displaced by an octave rather than creating a compact and smooth line in the bassoon. The right and left of the piano take on different variations of this bassoon line creating a contrapuntal texture that leads into a bassoon solo still utilizing large intervals. This leads into a section in a more dialogue-like texture through fragmentation that develops into a longer line. It unwinds into material similar to the opening to conclude the movement. The final movement “Slow” begins in a molto rubato style with a lyrical line that becomes more disjunct with larger intervals as it progresses and eventually jumping two octaves between figures. This leads to the final epilogue marked “steady” consisting of quarter note chords in the piano, which grace notes are added to later on. Briefly, some arpeggiation motifs from the first movement return. The bassoon plays a more restrained and lyrical line that begins with triplet eighth notes that unwinds to longer note values creating an introspective character to conclude the work.

description: This work is a five-movement suite based on Western Ukrainian folklore and music. The first movement “Carpathians is calling you” opens with a drone-type section on the pitch “D” that is interrupted with grace notes that grows and then dies away into a long silence. From the silence and dance-like melody inspired by Hutsul folk music emerges the occasionally gets thrown off by meter changes. The second movement “Morning in the mountains” is a slow lyrical melody in the tenor register that gradually expands with each sequence into a quasi-cadenza-like moment before restarting again now in the upper register. The third movement “Life of a wild forest” opens with a repeated staccato and grace note motif that grows and dies away twice. The second section is an uneven dance that is metrically grouped as 3+2 that features large intervallic jumps, flourishing runs, and double tonguing. The fourth movement “Interesting Hutsulian village” has an opening lyrical melody with an aggressive low register articulated section built on a motif of two beats of looping sixteenths and accented eighth notes that expands into a quasi-cadenza-like motive to return to a variation on the opening melody. The final movement “Dance with a beautiful Mavka” is an energetic and light waltz-like motif that gets interrupted by a measure of duple to depict the danger lurking for the young man dancing with the Mavka who according to folklore is unknowing being enticed and lured to his death.

description: This is a one-movement work with three main sections that takes inspiration from Ukrainian folklore and music and combines it with avant-garde language and idioms. The title Molfar comes from Hutsul culture and refers to men with supernatural abilities living in the forests of the Carpathian Mountains. Their abilities combine different elements of magic, fortune-telling, and healing. However, in oral stories throughout history, molfars have often been depicted as channeling their powers through black magic for evil purposes, which is demonstrated through the mysterious and aggressive characters that emerge from what begins as light and pure characters. Musically the piece takes inspiration from traditional Hutsul folk music utilizing the Ukrainian minor scale, which raises the 4th and 6th scale degrees on a natural minor scale, which is combined with contemporary rhythms, harmonies, and extended techniques such as multiphonic. The first section is a lyrical and mysterious melody in the bassoon that starts soft and grows over an erratic piano accompaniment depicting the beginning of a journey into the forests. This evolves getting more intense through increased motion in the piano accompaniment that leads into the next theme, which is a more aggressive staccato motif being traded between the bassoon and piano. Eventually, a variation of the opening melody returns in the bassoon that leads into a bassoon cadenza section with interruptions from the piano. During this cadenza section there are prepared piano interruptions to depict the evil character of the molfars attempting to take over. The final section of the piece is a fast and energetic dance-like motif that is taken from the fifth movement “Mavka” in Carpathian Sketches in triplet meter that gets interrupted by duple meter to depict a battle against the evil molfars.

description: This is a one movement work inspired by three quotes by Armenian poet and monk Grigor Narekatsi. The first section of the piece is based on a quote about how he offers his heart that is mourning to God for repentance. The second quote is asking for the Lord to hear the silence of his heart that is crying out and desiring mercy. The third quote is asking for the Lord to hear his prayers and to make him whole again through the sacrifice of salvation. The music is an evolution to depict this transformation in the speak. It begins with slow with contrapuntal lines weaving in and out of each other over top of long tones, which often are quarter tones providing an unstable base. It continues to intensify by increasing tempo, thicker textures, and the use of extended techniques. Eventually, the piece climaxes and a chant-like line emerges in the duduk that is joined by the oboe over drones in the other instruments symbolizing the acceptance of the speaker’s fate.

description: This work consists of nine short movements written in a style that combines elements of serialism and twelve-tone in a highly systemized way regarding pitch, rhythm, and tempo relations with melodic and rhythmic motifs from Ukrainian folk music. All of the movements, except five have just a metronome marking and no descriptive title. The first movement “quarter note equals 132” has two main motifs: 1) quarter note tied to an eighth with a sixteenth note rest followed by a slurred sixteenth to an eighth repeated twice 2) three beats of disjunct triplet eighth notes. The motifs are variated and fragmented throughout such as the first motif is played in reverse. Initially, the motifs are in dialogue that develop into a contrapuntal texture occurring together. The next movement “eighth note equals 132” presents a folk-like theme solo in the bassoon that utilizes a tone row. The horn enters with its own independent line related to the theme while the other woodwinds enter with the theme in a fugal texture in the order of clarinet, oboe, then flute. The following movement “quarter note equals 84” alternates between three different materials: 1) a lyrical theme in a homorhythmic texture, 2) a energetic staccato repeated sixteenth note theme, and 3) a theme that combines elements of both. The fourth movement “eighth note equals 144” is a duet between the flute and horn that features two independent lines that weave in and out of one another mainly consisting of quarter, eighth, and sixteenth notes. The next movement “Largo, quarter equals 40” is chorale-like mostly in a homorhythmic texture. The following movement “quarter equals 126” is a quirky dance-like character with a theme based around perfect fourth interval that alternates between duple and triple feel achieved through 2/4 and 3/8 metre changes. As the movement develops it becomes more contrapuntal with different accompaniment lines added underneath. The seventh movement “dotted quarter equals 72” combines staccato large interval eight note motifs with legato sixteenth in either ostinato or scalar motion together in different textures throughout. The eighth movement “quarter equals 58” takes two lines that are in dialogue with one another that join together after a quasi-cadenza flute moment into a homorhythmic passage to conclude the movement. The final movement “quarter note equals 144” is another quirky and energetic dance-like character that combines weaving around eighth notes with syncopated accompaniment figures in changing metres to destabilize the groove.

description: This is a one-movement work in a quick and lively tempo that utilizes the technique of double phasing. The opening of the piece features the flute and oboe phasing a cell together that consists of an eighth note motif that alternates between the pitches “G” and “B♭” with rest inserted. Simultaneously, the clarinet and bassoon are phasing another cell that is an eighth note on the pitch “G” followed by a rest. As the section progresses the two instruments in each of the cells become phased apart from one another at one rate, while simultaneously the whole ensemble becomes unphased at another rate. In measure 25, a new cell is started in the clarinet and bassoon based on a motif that includes ascending eighth notes followed by multiple repetitive eighth notes and eighth rests in a row. The clarinet begins this cell alone with the bassoon entering in the eleventh measure. All of this happens while the flute and oboe continue to phase apart in their original cell. In measure 59, the clarinet and bassoon present a lyrical melody that begins in long note values and gradually increases to quarter notes overtop of the flute and oboe until they finally come together. This leads to an unison statement of the flute and oboe cell by the whole ensemble that becomes unphased and eventually comes together for a final tutti statement of the motif leading to the final unison long note “G” to complete the piece.

description: This is a two-movement work in contrasting characters that uses elements of traditional classical form combined with a modernistic choice in harmony, often juxtaposing different tonal areas simultaneously. The first movement “Andante” has a lyrical character that opens with a short melodic fragment in a dialogue between the instruments in conflicting tonal worlds. The flute begins with a one-measure motif based around arpeggiation in D major, which the oboe responds with a variation of this motif that starts in the middle of the initial motif on the dotted quarter (or quarter tied) in a conflicting B♭ major. The other instruments play in a contrapuntal texture that utilizes fragments of the flute motif such as the perfect fifth and major third interval in the bassoon and the semitone motion in the horn. The section progresses by developing the material into a longer phrase and exploring more tonal areas, such as the next iteration of the motif in the flute is now a whole tone higher in E major and expanded longer. The other voices continue in the contrapuntal texture while presenting new material such as an arpeggiated eighth note line that weave around the harmony in the clarinet. Eventually, this develops into a section with new material consisting of a cascading line of arpeggiated quarter notes that are offset throughout the ensemble, beginning with thirds in the flute that become more disjunct through certain notes in the line being expands the interval such as a perfect fourth and by other notes being displaced from the expected octave such as instead of descending a third the note ascends a sixth creating a sense of instability until the music returns to material based off the opening section with some new variations to conclude the movement. The second movement “Allegretto” has an energetic character that opens with a melody borrowing motifs from Hutsul folk music is split between the oboe and flute consisting of eighth and sixteenth notes overtop of a syncopated accompaniment line of eighth notes in the clarinet, bassoon, and horn. The section develops by new material being introduced overtop of this texture, such as the flute playing a fragment and syncopated version of this melody that is offset by an eighth note from the melody. The next section presents a new melodic line in the flute comprised of four sixteenth notes leading to eighth notes. This is overtop of short fragments such as two slurred eight notes, four slurred sixteenth notes, or a variation of these two combined, which pass around the ensemble to create a larger and cohesive line. Eventually, the texture in the ensemble changes to syncopated quarter notes in the oboe, bassoon, and horn combined with a new countermelody in the clarinet mainly consisting of eighth notes that harmonically weave around. A return to the opening material occurs, but quickly variates to become similar to the secondary melody. The movement continues to alternate between material from the two themes until the work concludes.

description: In Levitin’s chamber and instrumental music there is often inspiration from his teacher, Shostakovich’s music demonstrated through the “dramatic opposition of aggressive motor rhythms, contemplative writing and dance rhythms, as well as by the overall finesse and economy of means.”59 This is a three-movement concerto. The first movement “Allegro ma non troppo” begins with a lyrical theme in the clarinet based on scalar and arpeggiated motion overtop of constant eighth notes in the orchestra. Eventually, the bassoon enters with the theme in canon to the clarinet. As it develops it becomes a more contrapuntal texture with the orchestral accompaniment becoming more active adding in scalar passages of sixteenth notes overtop of the eighth notes. An orchestral interlude leads into the second theme presented in the bassoon consisting of repeated sixteenth notes leading to scalar eighth notes overtop of eighth note chords on beat one and three in the orchestra. This develops in a very similar manner to earlier leading back to the main theme, which becomes fragments that pass between the soloists. This then comes together to create a homorhythmic section between the soloists with the orchestra playing a countermelody and eighth notes. The rest of the movement continues in this manner of presenting new themes or motifs that get developed using similar techniques with returns to the main theme until an “Andantino” return in the soloists with trills in the orchestra. This prompts a final virtuosic “Presto” section to conclude the movement. The second movement “Andantino” features a lyrical melody first presented in the clarinet with the bassoon joining in a canon overtop of quarter note chords on beat two and three and a dotted half note bass line in the orchestra. The final movement “Vivace” begins with an orchestral introduction that presents a playful eighth and sixteenth note theme. The movement shifts between this theme and a more lyrical theme throughout using similar textures and techniques of development. The majority of the movement is the soloists with prominent lines while the orchestra plays accompaniment figures.

description: This is a three-movement work in a neoclassical style that utilizes elements of sonata form combined with twentieth-century harmonic language in a style similar to Shostakovich. The first movement “Allegro non troppo” is in sonata form and opens with a lyrical main theme consisting of arpeggiated or scalar sixteenths that lead to a longer note value in the bassoon overtop of fragments of sixteenth notes in the right hand and a bass line in the left hand. This develops into the secondary theme based on a sequential passage of staccato sixteenth notes in the bassoon, which the piano echoes. This becomes a fragmented ostinato in the piano that the bassoon plays syncopated quarter notes overtop of before repeating to the beginning. One thing to note about the edition is the repeat is in different spots in the piano score and the bassoon part. It is incorrect in the score and the first ending should only be the last three measures and not the four measures written. The piano score the second time through should play the first measure of the first ending before going to the second ending. The development changes key to Eb minor and begins with a large interval motif in a lyrical style overtop of a chordal piano accompaniment. This is abruptly interrupted with material similar to the secondary theme in a canon-like texture that goes through development stages. The coda brings back material similar to the opening of the development to conclude the movement. The second movement “Andante” begins with a semplice melody in the left hand of the piano consisting of quarter and half notes. Eventually, the bassoon enters with a melody using elements from the opening such as tied quarter notes from beats 3 to 1. As it develops it intensifies, becoming eighth notes and ascending to the upper register of the bassoon. The movement continues developing and recombining the various themes, motifs and fragments of them together leading to a return to the opening material in the piano alone. The final movement “Allegretto” begins with the bassoon attacca overtop of a long note held over in the piano from the previous movement. The bassoon presents the theme by starting slow and accelerando into the allegretto tempo. The theme is a joyful and dance-like character of two slurred eighth notes leading to a staccato eighth. After the bassoon’s presentation the piano enters with the theme while the bassoon plays an accompaniment role of staccato eighth notes on the main beats outlining the harmonic progression. The melody continues passing back and forth until a virtuosic sixteenth note run appears out of nowhere in the piano. This leads into a disjunct and marcato line of eighth notes in the bassoon. The next section is an espressivo and vocal-like melody in the bassoon overtop of chordal eighth notes in the piano. Eventually, this gets combined with the opening theme and motifs, which ritenuendos into a poco meno mosso section that transforms the main theme into a legato and a dream-like quality from the lush harmonies. This is abruptly contrasted with a piano interlude consisting of thick staccato eighth note chords leading into an “Andante” section which has the disjunct eighth notes from earlier in a legato character in the piano that ends on an open fifth. The bassoon enters with a quasi-cadenza moment of rubato eighth notes in the upper register. A final “Allegro” section with marcato eighth notes in dialogue between the bassoon and piano occurs to conclude the work.

description: This is a short work that presents a theme in a vocal-like style in the middle register of the bassoon consisting of eighth, quarter and half notes in a moderato tempo with seven variations that are all attacca. The first variation “L’istesso tempo” consists of an eighth note followed by a sixteenth rest and note that outline notes from the theme. This develops into a line of consistent triplet eighth notes. The next variation also marked “L’istesso tempo” utilizes a motif of three eighth notes in a syncopated manner beginning on the second eighth note of the beat. The third variation “Andante” is an espressivo character that is slurred in the tenor and upper register of the bassoon. The following variation “L’istesso tempo” features a double dotted eighth note followed by a thirty-second note motif in an arpeggiated manner often with large intervals. The fifth variation “L’istesso tempo” are sextuplet sixteenth notes that weave around the main notes from the theme. The next variation “Allegretto” consists of arpeggiated staccato notes first played as eighth notes, which develops into sixteenth notes. The final variation “Tempo di valse” transforms the theme in a waltz character using two main rhythmic motifs:1) dotted quarter followed by an eighth leading to a quarter note motif throughout and 2) half note followed by a quarter note.

description: This is a four-movement suite that uses neoclassical structure combined with elements of folklorism such as melody, dance elements and harmony. The first movement “Romance” has a Da Capo form. The A section “Allegretto espressivo” features a lyrical main theme in the oboe overtop of half note bass line in the bassoon, and arpeggiated eighth notes in the clarinet. Eventually, the flute joins in on the melody a third above the oboe. This leads into the second theme which is also lyrical, but this time in the bassoon overtop of a falling thirds in eighth notes ostinato that changes harmony throughout, and a countermelody in the flute that joins later on. The B section has a playful staccato eighth note theme in the flute overtop of quarter note accompaniment in the ensemble. A brief chromatic passage of eighth notes in the clarinet bridges a return to the beginning material. The second movement “Waltz” features a spirited waltz-like melody in the lower register of the clarinet overtop of bass line on the downbeats in the bassoon and quarter notes on beats two and three in the flute and oboe. Eventually, the oboe takes over the theme and the flute introduces an espressivo countermelody. The movement continues to develop this material. The third movement “Song” is in an adagio tempo with a folk-like theme that gets passed around the ensemble beginning solo in the oboe. The movement continues providing variations such as different accompaniment figures or changing to a contrapuntal texture throughout, while exploring different key areas. The final movement “Dance” is in an allegretto tempo which consists of texture of a bass line, melodic content and accompaniment figures. Throughout the movement different themes are presented that become more virtuosic as it progresses beginning with an eighth and sixteenth note melody in the clarinet that later is contrasted by a triplet sixteenth melody in the flute. Eventually, fragments of the different themes and motifs are combined together leading to a final accelerando to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work that utilizes a variety of contemporary techniques to reinterpret the traditional structures of classical music through aleatoric sections and unconventional notation. The piece opens with an unmetered section where the left hand of the piano has a semitone aleatoric motif and sporadic right-hand fragments. This is combined with an improvised-like quasi cadenza line first in the flute, then the bassoon. As the section progresses the flute and bassoon lines become shorter and closer together to create a dialogue. The next section is metered consisting of one measure motif that is repeated with small changes over time in a sequence-like manner. This leads into a homorhythmic legato melody in the flute and bassoon overtop of a disjunct passage of sixteenth notes built on large intervals such as minor ninth. Eventually, this develops back into the opening quasi-cadenza material. However, this time the flute and bassoon are overlapping and interrupting each other.

description: This is a one-movement work and the first of Liashenko’s collection of technema works. This is a style of music that explores different timbres and color schemes to form a melody through micro-motifs and rhythmic displacements. The opening section of this piece features forte, accented dissonant chords with a horn repeated note motif that jumps a diminished fifth that is expanded outwards overtime. As it progresses the entry of each of the notes in the chord become displaced and staggered. Also, a triplet eighth motif that outlines different fourth intervals is introduced in the clarinet. This leads into the next section, which is aleatoric featuring a motif of disjunct sixteenths underneath variations of the motifs introduced thus far in the horn. Eventually, the oboe and clarinet join in on the triplet motif leading into the next section, which is a diminution of this motif on the sixteenth level. This is combined with a melody and a bass line to create a thicker texture. Next, the triplet motif is augmented into quarter notes and combined with fragments of the melodic line to create a new melody through these short fragmented micro-motifs being pieced together. The following section features the introduction of the final motif: two eighth notes in a third interval alternating between major and minor that get passed around the ensemble in a dialogue with unexpected pauses. The rest of the piece takes these micro-motifs continuing to vary and combine them with different possibilities exploring a wide range of timbres, colors and characters in the ensemble through only small changes to the material.

description: This is a one-movement Duo Concerto for oboe and bassoon written in the technema style. The form of the work is not in the typical concerto form. Instead, it has a couple main motifs that develop and come back unexpectedly. The opening texture has a dissonant cluster chord long-tone in the orchestra with two short motifs in the oboe and bassoon that are in dialogue with interjections from the vibraphone. The oboe motif is a legato line that weave around a minor third while the bassoon motif is a staccato arpeggiated line. The section develops and expands these motifs in a larger range and longer statement until it becomes contrapuntal, which the orchestra joins in on. Eventually, this winds down into one cohesive melody in the oboe with a clear accompaniment of counter-melody, inner harmony and bass line. The next section “Allegro moderato” features a trading sixteenth line between the oboe and bassoon that develops into being together while constantly switching between contrary and parallel motion. This is overtop of a homorhythmic accompaniment of fragments of eighth notes with rests in between each statement that eventually join the sixteenth note dialogue. Next, a return to the opening material returns followed by an orchestral interlude in a neoclassical style centered around an eighth note and triplet sixteenth motif. Afterwards, the soloists have improvisatory-like lines that are a beat apart in an echo manner overtop of an active scalar sixteenth note accompaniment. The next section consists of a lyrical line built around large intervals in the soloists overtop of drone texture that becomes more active and involved overtime. Eventually, the accompaniment becomes a line of staccato eighth notes that sets up the next section. The accompaniment has pizzicato string notes and short staccato figures in the winds underneath trading slurred eighth notes in the soloists. The soloists begin to incorporate elements of the accompaniment line until it becomes in unison with it. This leads into a new syncopated quarter note triplet motif in the soloists. As this starts to develop it morphs into a variation of the improvisatory-like lines that echo again, which the accompaniment winds begin to echo with a weaving line played on harmonics in the strings. This texture eventually becomes an orchestral interlude of homorhythmic sixteenth note passages. The piece concludes with a return to a variation of the opening material.

This proceeds to the second section which continues the weaving line but now it is an eighth against six texture with a different melody that begins in the flute until the oboe takes over and breaks the weaving texture shifting to a contrapuntal texture briefly. A new flute melody begins again over top of a long tone in the other voices which turns into a continuous line of a motif based around triplet sixteenths and an eighth, which develops overtime into a contrapuntal texture before returning to the opening material, this time a five against three texture and the solo line in the clarinet, which the horn takes over but augmented rhythmically. The second movement “Allegretto” takes a melody or a motif that is then echoed and combined throughout the ensemble in different textures often in a fugue-like character that loops while it develops creating a constant stream that proceeds into the next material. The third movement “Allegro assai” is in an ABA form. The first section is a constant stream of eighth notes throughout the ensemble combined with different melodies that are developed and fragmented through elements such as variation, changing meters, instrumentation, harmony and tonality. description: Loginov’s music has a desire to merge together sound ideas and meaning by having a complete openness to any known techniques by turning to theatricality with a synthesis of other art types. An important inspiration in his music is emotion and subconsciousness, which lead to a dream theme. He searches for ways to convey the mutual absorption of dreams and reality with self-reflection. Therefore, according to Loginov music is “primarily about communication, connection with people and the nature of things. In the broadest sense of these words.”60 The work itself utilizes graphic notation to convey various characters and emotions leaving lots of improvisation up to the performer. The score is structured using timestamps to move between the sections. For example, a diagram of circles is used to designate the inhaling and exhaling of air noises. For the multiphonic sections they are denoted with lines that zig zag in desired direction without specifying any specific pitches to be performed. Directions for double tonguing are given with “T-K” syllabus written overtop of the notes. This is also combined with short aleatoric motifs that are written out in between time stamps. All of these extended techniques, improvised sections, and aleatoric motifs are combined overtop of an electronic track. It first begins with static noises that gives the effect of white noise that a person would use to fall asleep to. Next, the track features a low bass drum like effect with animal noises that begin chaotic which become bird chirping. The track continues switching between more ominous noises and more nature-like rainfall to create contrasting characters as if going between a nightmare and a dream. Throughout a return to the static noise occurs to ground the listener.

description: This is a short one movement work in ternary form that explores the expressive and technical aspects of the bassoon. The A section “Adagio sostenuto” features a lyrical and vocal line mainly in scalar and arpeggiated motion that weaves around harmonically between key areas. As it progresses a string of articulated eighth notes accelerando with an abrupt return to the original tempo with fragmented material from earlier in a more aggressive character due to the introduction of accents. This then rallentando through a motif of eighth notes outlining harmony belonging to F♯ major with some chromaticism climaxes to a fermata whole note on the pitch “F♯”. ‘The B section “Piu mosso” has an improvisatory character consisting of disjunct line imitating two-voice writing. The poco rubato slurred sixteenth notes weave around in the lower register of the bassoon that lead tenuto-staccato eighth notes two and a half octaves higher in the tenor register. As it progresses the sixteenth passages become shorter and fragmented, and while the eighth note line is extended with sixteenth notes added beforehand. Eventually, this combined into one virtuosic line of sixteenths traversing the range of the bassoon arriving at a high C♯ fermata whole note. The return of the A section opens identical to the beginning of the piece but instead of developing and climaxing it fades away with a half note followed by a quarter note rest motif, which leads to a final dotted half note on the pitch “G” to conclude the work.

description: This is a four-movement programmatic work that follows a story of a unicorn in an avant-garde aesthetic. The work pushes the boundaries of instrumental technique and typical quintet playing through seeking new sounds and forms for musical ideas to settle in, which is achieved through the paradox of characters throughout. The first movement “Unicorn’s Song” is centered around a repeated note motif on the pitch “C” that each instrument is weaving together a different rhythm to create a constant stream of rhythm. This is combined with quartertones surrounding the pitch “C” to create unexpected dissonances creating a melody and effect that sounds like an animal call or cry. The second movement “Unicorn’s defile” has the character of an unbalanced dance with a constant changing of two versus three note grouping of the eighths combined with a melody of eighth notes and quarter notes that do not follow an expected pattern. The opening texture features a melody in the flute, countermelody in the oboe and accompaniment chords in the other voices. This evolves into a string of legato and constant eighth notes before arriving at a more staccato and syncopated eighth note line with the introduction of rests thrown in. This progresses until combining elements of both the legato and staccato motifs together. The movement continues alternating between these characters in the manner of a battle of dominance between the two. The next movement “Unicorn’s dance” is a disjointed line of sixteenths constantly trading off instruments after a couple notes with a couple short motifs emerging. The final movement “Unicorn’s games” features short cells of sixteenth note motifs that weave between the instruments to slowly expand and change over time in order to intensify and climax into the next section.

description: This is a five-movement suite that utilizes elements typical of Lyatoshynsky’s writing in the 1940s that was criticized as being formalist. It features introspective melodies that are woven out of short phrases, which emerge out of motifs that use rhythmic and dynamic waves allowing the music to open up as it naturally develops. Another aspect is the incorporation of folk music elements such as melodic and rhythmic ideas that are incorporated into romantic and expressionistic styles. The first movement “Moderato” features a vocal-like melody first presented by a solo oboe, which joined in the middle of the first period of the phrase with a contrapuntal texture. Throughout the movement the melody passes around the ensemble and a driving triplet eighth note motif in arpeggiated and sequential manner is introduced creating rhythmic dissonant against the eighth notes in the melody. Eventually, a return to the opening texture returns with triplet eighth notes introduced into the melody to create a cohesion of the competing motifs to conclude the movement. The next movement “Andante” opens in the same fashion as the previous movement with a vocal-like melody this time in the solo clarinet that gets passed around. The flute and bassoon enter with interjections that develops into a contrapuntal texture. Another driving rhythmic triplet eighth note ostinato is introduced in the middle section. This time the third and first note of each beat tied together featuring the intervals of an octave on the first beat and lower chromatic neighbour on the second beat. The third movement “Allegretto scherzando” is in ternary form. The A section has each of the different parts enter separately allowing the music to build naturally. First, a bass line in the bassoon is presented. Next, a countermelody in the clarinet and flute is added, and finally a melody in the oboe joins in. For the second phrase the flute and oboe switch roles. Next, a fragmented motif of four eighth notes that get traded around and developed into a cohesive new theme. This leads into a rhythmic motif that unwinds into the B section “Meno mosso, tranquillo” featuring two independent lines in a cantabile character that weave in and out of one another in the clarinet and bassoon. Eventually, the flute joins in on these themes with the oboe resting the entire section. A fragment of one of the themes is presented in the clarinet that slowly changes to a staccato character while it accelerandos to prepare the return to the A section. The following movement “Lento ma non troppo” opens with a theme in a period with an espressivo character in the solo clarinet. For the second half of the period the bassoon enters with a countermelody. As the movement continues the theme is passed around with more countermelodies being added creating a thicker texture. After the climax, a chorale section occurs to conclude the movement. The final movement “Allegro” opens with a short fugal section as an introduction with the theme beginning in the bassoon followed by the clarinet, oboe, and finally flute. Afterwards, the main theme of the movement is presented in the clarinet, which is a cantabile and vocal-like melody overtop of a staccato eighth note bass line in the bassoon. Immediately after the second theme is presented in the oboe overtop of the same texture. Throughout the movement these themes are fragmented and combined in different textures. To conclude the movement a virtuosic sixteenth note passage emerges in the clarinet that leads into a chain of sixteenths passing around the ensemble beginning in the low register of the bassoon until it arrives in the upper register of the flute followed by a final G minor chord to conclude the work.

description: This is a four-movement suite utilizing structures and phrasing from neoclassical with contemporary harmonic language. The first movement “Minuetto” is in a moderato tempo is an unbalanced minuet in 7/8 that switches note groupings each bar throwing off the natural flow expected. For example, the opening measures are 3+2+2 followed by 2+2+3. It is in a contrapuntal texture without a clear theme being repeated. Instead, different short motifs are linked together. The next movement “Intermedio” is in an allegro tempo that features a couple motifs utilized throughout. There are disjointed eighth notes jumping around, accented quarter notes in a scalar and sequential motion, and a dotted quarter note followed by an eighth note in an arpeggiated motion. Texturally, the flute and oboe are homorhythmic the entire movement in contrast to the bassoon. The third movement “Adagio” is contrapuntal presenting a melody in the flute, accompaniment figures in the oboe and a bass line in the bassoon. At the reprise of the theme at the end the oboe takes over for the first half of the phrase before handing it back off to the flute. The final movement “Gigue” is in a vivo tempo and is an energetic dance in ternary form using a Da Capo al Coda. The A section has a theme based on dotted eighth notes overtop of a sequential triplet sixteenth motif involving large intervals. The B section combines the melody and triplet sixteenth motif into one line into three different variations for each voice creating a contrapuntal texture.

premiere: in summer 2025
description: Malyi’s compositions are structured and inspired by utilizing a different method or technique for each specific work to shape the musical material. This work takes inspiration from Pre-Christian aesthetics and songs through the use of polymodality, texture such as heterophonic passages, and timbre. However, it uses newly composed motifs and materials. This is combined with an alternative approach to development by using motif variation, which a similar approach can be seen in works by composers such as Stravinsky, Bartok, and Ligeti. The alternative development is combined with a combination method utilizing elements of polyphony techniques and minimalism. Specifically, almost all of the time throughout the work there is the dichotomy between stable and unstable that is often expressed through a main stable voice in an ostinato texture interacting with secondary unstable voices in a changing counterpoint texture. The first movement “Allegro vivace” opens with the main motif in the flute consisting of four notes in descending stepwise motion with the last note changing interval such as a major third and augmented fourth. This motif is consistent throughout the movement with small variations as it gets passed around the ensemble for each section. The rest of the ensemble’s accompaniment figures become more contrapuntal and rhythmically active as the movement develops. The next movement “Andante con moto” is based around a motif that is built by each note being played by a different voice to create a larger line. The opening section is built on longer note values that pass around the ensemble, which sound closer together as it progresses until the first note of one voice lines up with the last one of the preceding voice and eventually overlapping creating a thicker texture. At the end of the section frullato is introduced to create more variety in the timbre and texture. The next section begins with staccato eighth notes in a consistent chain of one after another. Eventually, the eighths develop into two sixteenth notes and develops into a larger main motif played in one voice consisting of eighth, two sixteenth, eigth, and quarter note. As it reaches the climax the voices overlap like the previous section to conclude the work. The third movement “Moderato” begins with the main motif played by the oboe comprised rhythmically of eighth and quarter notes that is a continual ascend to the peak of the motif. The clarinet provides accompaniment figures of a longer note leading to a staccato eighth note. Next, the bassoon takes over the main motif with the clarinet dropping out of the texture while the flute joins in with a new accompaniment figure creating a contrapuntal texture in the ensemble. Afterwards, the clarinet re-enters with a variation of the main motif with a homorhythmic texture in the rest of the ensemble of accented eighth notes to create a syncopation and to destabilize the metres. The motif gradually is expanded into a passage of ascending stepwise sixteenth notes, while the texture becomes more contrapuntal as it continues until returning to a more transparent texture of material passing around the ensemble to conclude the movement. The fourth movement “Andante moderato” is built around three main motifs 1) thirty-second note followed by a dotted eigth, 2) a whole tone scalar motif, and 3) a chromatic sixteenth note passage introduced in measure 161 by the clarinet. These motifs interact and develop independently of one another. They also get recombined and fragmented throughout creating a variety of different textures. Eventually, this climaxes into a virtuosic flute passage of sextuplets that becomes fragmented to conclude the movement. The final movement “Veloce” is comprised of two main motifs that are alternated between. The first motif is a whole tone scale that is in a texture of a scale of sixteenths that rotate around the ensemble in different note groupings such as the flute plays six sixteenth notes before passing to the clarinet that plays four sixteenth notes. The other motif has a more dance-like quality as it consists of staccato eighths leading to an offbeat accent that is tied creating a syncopated quality. This motif is also more vocal-like adding to the dance-like character. The rest of the movement continues developing these motifs such as the sixteenth notes becoming sextuplet sixteenths notes in a neighbour tone motion. Over time, the various developments from throughout are combined to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work that explores a wide variety of textures a wind quintet can achieve through extended techniques combined with three short fragments looped on a tape. However, the first half of the work is solely acoustic with the first fragment appearing in the middle of the work. The opening section consists of a weaving atonal line that has slight variations played simultaneously with accompaniment of multiphonics and frullato to distort the texture slightly. As the work progresses the ensemble gets more contrapuntal with increasing moments of rhythmic dissonant alongside a larger variety of extended techniques occurring simultaneously adding in quarter tones, singing and playing, and trills both half and whole tone. The next main section is a section feature long notes either straight tone or with a technique while the oboe performs glissandos on the reed detached from the instrument creating a sighing effect in the texture. This leads into the first fragment of the tape being utilized overtop of key clicks which instruct the performers to slowly raise their instruments above their heads while doing so. The final fragment tape section begins with repeated ostinato in straight tone, which becomes frullato as the tape enters. This later becomes air noises to conclude the piece.

description: This is a one-movement work in ternary form in a modernist style and aesthetic. The A section “Andante” opens with a fugal texture with a lyrical theme using a twelve-tone row presented first in the clarinet followed by the bassoon and violin. Eventually, a new theme using a different twelve-tone row is presented in the bassoon while the other voices continue in a fugal texture playing the original theme. The other voices over time depart from the main theme into new material in a more contrapuntal texture. This leads into a bassoon solo consisting of a descending slurred and lyrical line followed by tenuto quarter notes with rests in the bottom octave. The B section “Allegro vivace” is in a rondo form with a quirky and energetic character from the staccato and pizzicato eighth notes, repeated articulated sixteenth notes, and virtuosic slurred scalar motion sixteenths. This section is in a contrapuntal texture developing the theme and motifs presented at the beginning of the section. This leads into a bassoon solo introducing a new theme consisting of a scalar sextuplet, large intervals first articulated and then slurred interrupted by a eighth and two sixteenth motif. The clarinet and then violin enter in cannon with this theme with slight variations such as the clarinet playing the parts of theme in a different order. This develops into an ostinato consisting of different slurred large intervals in the clarinet and weaving quarter notes in the bassoon. Once the violin finished their phrase this prompts the clarinet and bassoon to play a fragment of the first three beats of theme in unison overtop of the ostinato in the violin. Eventually, the texture changes with the clarinet continuing the fragment with accompaniment figures in the violin and bassoon leading back to the material from the beginning of the allegro vivo returning. Afterwards the weaving quarter note line takes over combined with a new virtuosic arpeggiated motif in the violin eventually becoming scalar into another return of the opening allegro vivo material. This leads into a “Ritmico” section featuring a vocal-like line in the clarinet, rhythmic ostinato in the violin and a syncopated motif in the bassoon. The final section consists of solo scalar passages interrupted by dissonant tutti chords leading into an ominous bassoon solo reminiscent of earlier linking into the return of the A section.

description: This is a two-movement suite in a neoclassical style with clear forms and hierarchy of parts with melodic and rhythmic influence from folk music. The first movement is in ternary form in d minor. The A section “Moderato” opens with a lyrical folk-like theme in the bassoon overtop of syncopated accompaniment figures in the flute and clarinet. Eventually, the clarinet takes over the melody while the bassoon plays a chromatic half note bass line leading into a short homorhythmic section to bridge into the theme being played by the flute while a trading countermelody is passed being the oboe and bassoon to create a more contrapuntal texture. The B section is an “Allegretto” in a folk dance-like character and presents a secondary theme consisting of eighth and sixteenth notes leading to a quarter note overtop of a chromatic quarter note line in the oboe and clarinet. As the section progresses the accompaniment becomes more active. First, a syncopated eighth note motif than passages of scalar and arpeggiated sixteenth notes. The second movement “Allegretto scherzando” is in rondo form. The A section opens with a theme in the flute, accompaniment motifs in the oboe and clarinet, and a bass like in the bassoon. This develops into a dialogue of a fragment of the melody trading between the flute overtop of the original texture. This leads into the B section marked “subito piano” that is a homorhythmic passage of staccato eighth notes beginning tutti amongst the entire ensemble developing into a trading off texture before returning to tutti. The C section is a motif of quarter, two eighths, two quarters in the flute, oboe, and clarinet overtop of a rhythmic variation of this motif in the bassoon. The D section marked “meno mosso” has a lyrical and legato melody in the lower range of the bassoon overtop of an eighth note ostinato in the flute and oboe with a dotted quarter note line in the clarinet. This develops into a cannon of the melody in the flute and bassoon overtop of the ostinato motif. This material then becomes fragmented and developed before a DC al fine returning to the A through C sections.

description: This is a suite of six short movements also in a neoclassical style with folk influence. The first movement “Introduction” in a grave tempo features a dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth motif first introduced in the horn that is echoed by the rest of the ensemble as the horn holds a long note. This texture continues for the rest of the movement with one group playing the motif while the other holds a long note. The second movement “Allegro scherzando” is in ternary form. The A section is mostly a homorhythmic texture of eighth notes and rests with the occasional solo line emerging from the texture. The B section features a solo line that passes around overtop of accompaniment figures in the rest of the ensemble that begin as dotted quarter notes and develop into the opening rhythmic motif of eighth note, eighth rest, eighth note that sets up the return to the A section. The following movement “Ritornello” is in a grave maestoso tempo featuring a motif in dialogue similar to the opening movement with an additional measure of quarter notes leading to a whole note to provide the harmonic functions necessary to conclude the movement. This goes attacca into the fourth movement “Andante con moto” consisting of a folk-like melody, accompaniment figures, and a bass line which the roles pass around the ensemble. The next movement “Ritornello” has a lively character beginning with a four-measure section in an echo texture that then becomes homorhythmic for the rest of the movement. It is centered around an eighth and quarter note motif. The final movement “Finale” is in rondo form with three statements of the virtuosic theme comprised mainly of sixteenth notes is contrasted with episodes that revisit material from the previous movements.

This work consists of five short movements in contrasting characters. The first movement “Adagio” has a dolce espressivo melody first presented in the oboe overtop of a long tone accompaniment motif in the clarinet. The melody passes around the ensemble as the texture gets more contrapuntal as more voices enter. There is a middle section that presents a eighth note and rests motif that is homorhythmic in texture. The movement concludes with fragments of the main theme, accompaniment motif, and eighth note motif all combined in the flute, oboe, and clarinet. The next movement “Allegro non troppo” has three main components that are combined together: 1) a repeated sixteenth motif, 2) a syncopated sixteenth note and rest motif, and 3) a lyrical line of long notes. The third movement “Tempo di marcia” opens with the clarinet solo imitating a bugle call playing arpeggiated triplet eighth notes. Accompaniment figures in the ensemble take over leading into the main theme in a march-like style built around a dotted eighth and sixteenth note motif presented in the horn. The theme is fragmented and passed around the ensemble and combined with a lyrical line. There is a brief interrupting middle section “Tempo di polka” consisting of a melody in the flute and offbeats in the other voices. The following movement “Largo espressivo” consists of different ad libitum solos often in a virtuosic manner in dialogue throughout the ensemble. The final movement “Allegro” is centered around a main theme that passes around the ensemble with accompaniment figures. As the movement progresses the texture becomes more active and contrapuntal, developing into a sixteenth scalar ostinato combined with a chorale-like melody leading to a final two chords to conclude the work.
