description: This is a one-movement work that pushes the technical boundaries of the bassoon virtuosity and extended techniques to create a wide range of textures and tonal possibilities to display the concept of synapse. It consists of two worlds working together to produce one unified result. Often, in the work a contrast and switch between textures occurs. The work begins with a long tone that introduces fast articulated notes briefly in the middle of the note to contrast between a calmer and more frantic texture. This then becomes a short ostinato passage in a chromatic manner that becomes more chaotic through accelerando beaming. This continues to alternate with the opening texture which sequences higher in the bassoon range. Eventually, new material is presented with the introduction of new textures with slap tonguing, frullato and con sordino. As it develops the fragmented motifs return to bring in the contrasting characters and worlds again. However, this time the fragmentations become connected into a longer phrase with no rests in between each iteration becoming more and more virtuosic with each successive return. The work concludes with the longer note value and calmer texture but now interrupted with rests, as if the synapses are breaking down returning to their separate worlds.

description: This work is structured around fifteen repeated sections that the performers progress through. The work opens with a cadenza in the first bassoon in a virtuosic manner with large intervals and sudden dynamic shifts from forte to piano. The first two sections feature a texture of drones underneath and an aleatoric motif in the first bassoon and a melodic line with written out ornamentation in the second bassoon. The next two sections combine four different short motifs that interact around the ensemble. The fifth and sixth sections are mainly homorhythmic statements. The fifth is more rhythmic, comprised of thirty second notes leading to an eighth note while the sixth is more lyrical with longer notes in a syncopated manner. The following two sections alternate between homorhythm and brief canonic entrances. The ninth section is a rhythmic dialogue between the voices. The tenth section features drones in the third and fourth bassoon while the second bassoon has a string of sextuplet sixteenth notes with the sixth of each grouped accented and tied to the next beat overtop of an ostinato triplet quarter followed by a eighth on the pitch “C”. The next section takes the sextuplet and disjuncts it and creates rhythmic dissonance by introducing competing oscillating thirty-second notes in the third bassoon. The twelfth section consists of quarter notes that are disjunct and switch between fortissimo and mezzo-piano dynamics in the first and section bassoon, while the other bassoons hlonger note values. The following section combines two rhythmic ostinatos in the third and fourth bassoon, while the first bassoon has a melodic line, and the second bassoon has aleatoric material. This climaxes to an improvised section in the for the second, third, and fourth bassoon overtop of a whole note on the pitch “G” in the first bassoon. The fourteenth section consists of drones in the ensemble with a disjunct line of thirty seconds in the second bassoon. The final section has different rhythmic ostinato patterns that are rhythmically dissonant to one another as there are triplet sixteenths, dotted eighth notes, and quadruple eighth notes in a 6/8-time signature.

description: This is a one-movement work in an unmetered style but with dashed bar-lines throughout to indicate phrases and sections to give a sense of structure to the performer.  Overall, the work features virtuosic passages that often begin as an ostinato that undergoes small changes over time until it reaches a climax. It begins in a calm character with air noise effects before the first fragment of thirty-second notes is introduced which leads to longer note values. As it develops the motifs get stringed together creating a long line allowing for a larger phrase to emerge. Over time the motifs become more disjunct and aggressive through larger intervals and quick repeated and articulated notes, in the manner that a virus would take over as it becomes stronger as it infiltrates its surroundings. Eventually, the motifs begin to break down as rests are unexpectedly inserted without an obvious pattern symbolizing the breakdown caused by a virus. The work continues breaking down in this manner until a rest is between almost every single note allowing for the original air noise texture to return. After the longest rest in the entire work of almost two quarter notes a final fermata air noise note that dies away to niente occurs like a victim taking its final breath before a virus wins.

description: This is a four-movement suite in a neoclassical style that utilizes typical form and conventions while exploring elements of consonance and atonality within the ensemble. The first movement “Prelude” opens with a declamatory motif of dotted eighth note followed by a sixteenth note leading to a longer note in a canon entrance in a cluster chord. This prompts a virtuosic staccato sextuplet response in the flute. After a grand pause the next section features a semplice theme in the flute overtop of accompaniment figures in the ensemble. A return of the opening material occurs an octave higher moprhing into triplet motifs from the semplice theme throughout the ensemble. The next movement “Fugue” presents a slurred theme that weaves around the tonic pitch “F” played first by the oboe. A modulation to F♯ occurs to transition into a contrasting playful section that consists of staccato arpeggiated motion that leads to a perfect fourth non-staccato motif. Eventually the opening theme returns in a staccato articulation and rests inserted for the second half of longer note values, such as quarter note becoming eighth note followed by an eighth rest played by the clarinet. This is followed by a return to the original theme played in homorhythm and contrary motion. It is then fragmented and passed around the ensemble. Another contrasting section occurs with a vocal-like melody in the flute, arpeggiated eighth notes in the oboe and clarinet, and a bass line in the bassoon. A final fugal section occurs to conclude the movement. The third movement “Canon” presents eighth notes leading to a longer note value that oscillates a ascending minor third interval first played by the flute alone. This is followed by entrances in the oboe and then clarinet, which each entrance is accompanied by an increase in the tempo. This material continues to be developed leading into a slower contrasting section that is a variation on the motif. It is repeated quarter notes leading to a descending minor third. The movement continues to develop the material as it speeds back up. The final movement “Cadenza and Chorale” features a chorale consisting of eighth, quarter, and half notes in a mostly step-wise motion in the oboe, clarinet, and bassoon, which is mostly in homorhythm with occasional moments of counterpoint. This is combined with a virtuosic staccato sextuplet alternating octaves on the pitch “E” in the flute. The ensemble gradually accelerando throughout the movement before abruptly returning to the opening tempo. A final section that brings back material from the opening of the first movement concludes the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work in a jazz style that features a head (melody) with some variations throughout to imitate the idea of improvisation in the clarinet and bassoon. This is overtop of a texture of a stereotypical jazz combo of piano, guitar, bass, and drums. However, Novokhatsky also includes a classical element of a chordal accompaniment played by a viola, which is unusual in jazz idioms. The work opens with a brief accompaniment introduction with typical jazz motifs played by the combo to set up a bossa nova feel for the piece. The bassoon then enters with the head that is based around the perfect fifth interval. Eventually, the clarinet enters as the head begins to undergo slight variations. The texture between the clarinet and bassoon is mostly homorhythmic in unison or consonant harmonies such as a perfect fifth. Next, the clarinet becomes more virtuosic playing a string of eighth notes that noodle around while the bassoon plays a more arpeggiated and bass line passage underneath, which is a variation of the double bass line. Eventually, a return to the original head in similar texture occurs to bridge into another variation. Finally, another return to the head occurs with a brief coda in the combo of jazz idioms to conclude the work occurs.

description: This is a virtuosic six-movement suite as a homage for Francisco Goya, who was a Spanish romantic painter that reflected the historical upheavals and influenced generations of composers. The title refers to his collection of 80 prints using the technique of aquatint published in 1799. Goya described that the themes of the works come from the “extravagances and follies common to all society”69 depicting well-known persons of the time. The work is structured on a variety of different sections in each movement that is inspired by a certain picture from the collection combined together to create a cohesive piece. The first movement is slow marked eighth note equals 68 and begins with a section titled “Francisco Goya y Lucientes Paintor” which is the first of the 80 in the collection and it is a self-portrait of Goya. Musically, it features a half note tied to a dotted eighth note followed by a sixteenth leading to a dotted half note played on the contrabassoon, which is echoed in the piano. As it develops the piano responses become thicker and more active. The next section “The say “I will” and give their hand to the first coming” consists of an oscillating sixteenth note cluster chord motif in the piano. This becomes fragmented and the bassoon interjects in the rests often with one to three sixteenth notes. The following section “Here comes the bogey-man” consists of short sixteenth note fragments of either two sixteenths or three triplet sixteenth notes separated by rests in a homorhythmic texture. Afterwards “Nanny’s boy” section is rhythmically dissonant with repeated duple eighth notes in the left hand of the piano competing with arpeggiated triplet eighth notes in the bassoon. Eventually, the roles reverse. The final section “Tantalus” consists of arpeggiated sextuplets with two notes in a row before changing in the bassoon overtop of a disjunct and rhythmically dissonant piano accompaniment. The second movement is also slow marked quarter note equal 63. The first section “That dust” and second section “There was no help” consists of multiphonic long notes in the bassoon marked pianissimo underneath a rhythmically complex piano line marked fortissimo that continually ascends and descends. The next section “He broke the pitcher” brings back the two sixteenth notes motif leading to scalar runs with eighth note interjections in the piano in between the bassoon’s fragments. The final section “They already go plucked” expands the scalar runs into a full phrase with contrapuntal lines in the piano. The third movement is marked dotted half note equals 40 and begins with the section “Fine advice” consisting of an oscillating major second in eighth and quarter note triplets with a contrapuntal line in the piano that switches between triplets and dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth note motifs throughout. The next section “Should God forgive her. She was her mother…” takes the motifs that were expanded and puts them homorhythmic in the bassoon and right hand of the piano overtop of a syncopated bass line in the left hand. The final section “Hush” brings back the original piano line combined with a weaving sixteenth note line in the bassoon that ends with the bassoonist saying “Shhh” to conclude the movement. The fourth movement is marked quarter equals 60 and opens with the “They spruce themselves up” section that has sixteenth note motifs in dialogue between the bassoon and piano. The next section “They are warm” is based around a slurred descending interval that becomes larger overtime in the contrabassoon that the piano responds with four cluster chord eighth notes. The final section “The chichillas” features repeated articulated sixteenth notes in the contrabassoon with eighth note chords in the piano. The fifth movement is marked quarter note equals 60 opening with the section “Will the disciple be wiser?” is a dialogue of quarter and half notes between the contrabassoon and piano alternating when they change notes. The final two sections “Bravissimo” and “Thou who canst not” are marked quarter equals 126 and it is an energetic dance-like character with an energetic bass line ostinato and offbeat chords in the piano and melody in the contrabassoon that switches between beginning on the beat and syncopated. The final movement is marked eighth equals 63 and begins with the “And they still won’t go” section brings back material from the very opening of the piece. The following section “Squealers” continues the same piano accompaniment while the contrabassoon plays a melody while crowing a pitch on the reed in their mouth simultaneously. The next section “It is time up” is an aggressive and rhythmic character in a contrapuntal texture. The final section “The dream of reason brings forth monsters” consists of a long tone on the low Bb in the contrabassoon while the piano plays a disjunct accompaniment to conclude the work.

description: This is a three-movement work as a homage to Spanish artist Pablo Picasso who is known as one of the founders of the Cubism movement. This movement rejected traditional techniques such as perspective and foreshortening in favor of emphasizing the flat, two-dimensional surface of the picture’s plane. This created a new reality that depicted radically fragmented objects. (Britannica “Cubism”) The first movement “Lento” begins with long tones in the winds with the texture of the flute beginning the phrase and the bassoon entering on their second note a perfect fifth below and then moving in between each of the flute’s notes in similar motion. Next, the piano enters a semitone a minor ninth above the bassoon creating dissonance. The piano changes into between the two winds creating a canon-like effect. Eventually, the instruments come together in a homorhythmic texture leading to a fermata half note rest. This is followed by a return to the previous canon-like texture with the piano playing cluster chords in voiced in open spacing. The second movement “Allegro moderato” features a disjunct staccato eighth note ostinato in the piano underneath virtuosic passages of sixteenth notes in the winds. Later, the roles reverse between the piano and the winds. Eventually, a more chordal eighth note accompaniment is introduced. As the movement develops the roles continue to change around in different combinations of instrumentation. The final movement is built around a main motif that slowly gets altered throughout. The opening section “Andante” consists of chords in the piano with a one measure motif of two eighth notes leading to a quarter note followed by an eighth and half note in the flute that starts in the middle of the measure. The next section “Adagio” takes the motif being and slightly compresses it by changing the half note to a quarter note to make it into a one measure ostinato in 7/8 spelling out A major, while the flute plays a lyrical melody overtop of it. Eventually, the metre shifts to 8/8 adding a third eighth note to the beginning of the motif. As it develops and the metre changes to 12/8 the motif becomes expanded in the piano, while the bassoon introduces a countermelody consisting of eight notes weaving around. Eventually, the weaving line becomes staccato in the winds and is played overtop of chords in the piano. A return to the “Andante” section occurs to conclude the work.

description: This is a one movement work that is structured as a theme with seven variations. The opening theme “Morendo” presents the theme in the clarinet consisting of mainly eighth, quarter, half, and dotted half notes. The violin and bassoon provide accompaniment support underneath with short rhythmic motifs. The first variation “Moderato” rhythmically augments and adds virtuosic ornamentation such as sixteenth note sextuplets to the theme played by the violin. The clarinet plays a syncopated ostinato on a repeated pitch, while the bassoon plays the occasional bass note. The next variation “Allegro animato” has a contrapuntal texture with elements of theme weaving between the instruments, while it alternates character from a playful staccato character to lyrical legato. The following variation “Cantabile” turns the theme in a vocal-like line that passes around the ensemble overtop of an arpeggiated eighth note line. Eventually, a syncopated bass line is introduced in the bassoon after its turn at the melody and accompaniment line. Variations four through six have no description marking, but a metronome marking is provided. The fourth variation marked quarter note equals 100-110 turns the theme into triplets in an arpeggiated manner in the clarinet and violin overtop of accompaniment figures in the bassoon. The next variation is marked quarter note equals 70-80, which fragments the theme combining elements together in different combinations. The following variation is marked quarter note equals 80-90 consisting of the theme being passed around by each instrument only playing a couple of the notes at a time before passing off to another. It is also in a more disjunct and staccato character. The final variation “Allegro non troppo” brings back elements from throughout the work such as the syncopated repeated note line combining them once last time to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work in an allegretto con moto tempo that utilizes classical forms such as rondo and a theme with various episodes in the form of ABACAD. It opens with a two-measure motif that consists of staccato eighth notes with slurred grace notes before the second and third beats in the lowest register of the bassoon. Then, in the third measure the piano enters with a counter melody that leads to development of the motif into a full phrase with an increase in range and rhythmically adding quarter and sixteenth notes. The texture of the piano switches to accompaniment providing chordal support with short interjections in the right hand. Next, a contrasting B section in the same tempo occurs where two different time signatures occur simultaneously, 3/4 in the bassoon and 6/8 in the piano. This section is a playful melody in the bassoon overtop of a chordal piano accompaniment that sounds syncopated due to the conflict of time signatures creating moments of rhythmic dissonance that resolve. Then a return to the A section occurs but develops differently to climax into a virtuosic quality with constant scalar sixteenths in unison in the bassoon and piano. Next, another contrasting C section occurs in an Andante con anima tempo, which has a legato, more vocal-like melody that occurs in a cannon starting with the bassoon followed by the right-hand, and then left-hand of the piano. Another return to the A material occurs. This is followed by another contrasting D section in an allegro tempo. This is a virtuosic section that showcases the bassoon’s technical capabilities through a string of sequencing sixteenth notes overtop of an accompaniment piano part that occasionally interjects with sixteenths. Finally, one last statement of the A material occurs to conclude the piece.

description: This is a three-movement work that includes idioms from avant-garde and neoclassical that are in opposition. Overall, Pavensky’s music is characterized by diversity through the inclusion of polystylistic elements using a neoclassical musical language and folk inspiration while experimenting with elements of avant-garde aesthetics, twelve-tone, and sonorism. The first movement “Prologue” is in an allegro ma non troppo tempo opens in a neoclassical style presenting a theme in dialogue between two groups. First the flute and oboe at a mezzoforte dynamic that is echoed by the clarinet, bassoon, and horn at mezzopiano. Eventually, the two groups come together playing in unison which is contrast with short sections of contrapuntal writing. This leads into a “Meno mosso Scherzando” section consisting of a bassoon solo with short fragment interjections from the upper winds. This develops into an avant-garde section in a thick contrapuntal texture with short solos that emerge overtop of this texture. The theme and motifs presented continue developing and slowly increasing in tempo until returning to a reprise of the opening material. The second movement “Minuet” opens with chorale-style quarter notes in the ensemble that are in an atonal harmony which are interrupted with brief moments that are tonal in a Viennese Waltz style. This leads into a polytonality section where each instrument plays an independent line each in a different key signature (flute C major, oboe A major, clarinet Gb major, bassoon G major, and horn F major) that is weaving in and out of one another. Next, a theme is played in cannon around the ensemble that leads into a development of the Viennese Waltz material presented earlier that climaxes in a a chain of chromatic sixteenth notes building in score order to a trilled fermata note. This is immediately contrasted by unconventional air noises. A reprise of the opening section occurs that leads into a flute cadenza to end the movement. The final movement “Epilogue” is in an allegretto con moto tempo opening with a homorhythmic forte passage. This leads into a section where eighth notes trade around the ensemble to create a larger, more cohesive line. This is interrupted by moments of homorhythmic fragments. Next, a clarinet solo is presented overtop of a contrapuntal texture. Eventually, a return to the minuet material from the previous movement occurs to set up an aleatoric section. This is contrasted by a neoclassical section before more second movement material returns. Finally, the neoclassical dominates and a full minuet section with all of the stereotypical and required elements is presented to conclude the piece.

description: This is a three-movement work that “displays a chain of emotional states from the lyrical and romantic mood at the beginning through restlessness and rhythmic instability in its middle movement to the concluding mediation and apprehension of the past developments.”73 The formula for this piece is “epitomizing the objective principle and entering into a dialogue by playing its weighty phrases in counterpoint with the solo part.”74 The first movement “Lento” opens with a lyrical bassoon solo that weaves around the pitch “D” with some incorporation of quarter tones. The strings enter with longer note value dissonant chords, while the bassoon them continues to expand and develop. Eventually, when the bassoon switches to a smorzato section the strings become contrapuntal, which leads into a short virtuosic bassoon cadenza. The strings re-enter playing fragments of the quintuplet sixteenth notes from the cadenza in a canon-like texture. This continues developing until a climax of a rhythmic dissonant accented repeated note that ends abruptly as the bassoon holds over into a fermata note. The movement continues revisiting the earlier material and textures presented. The second movement “Tempo libro” is unmetered using note heads with a black line leading to the next event to connect together fragments of quicker note value or accelerando beamed groups. These fragments rapidly pass around the ensemble creating a larger cohesive line. Eventually, “Allegro agitato” section in 3/4 metre occurs consisting of fragmented motifs leading to a long note that is often trilled in a contrapuntal texture. This leads into a bassoon cadenza featuring virtuosic passages leading to an extended technique such as frullato or multiphonic. The final movement “Lento” is reminiscent of the first movement bringing back the themes, motifs and textures.

description: This is a one-movement work in memory of Denisov, who was Pavlenko’s teacher at the Moscow Conservatory. The work explores avant-garde style and techniques associated with Denisov. The work opens with a “Poco adagio” section that features a dialogue-like texture with a lyrical line in the bassoon with fragmented responses in the piano during the bassoon’s longer note values. As it develops the texture becomes contrapuntal with three-stave writing in the piano occurring. The next section “Poco agitato” returns to a dialogue-like texture with virtuosic thirty-second note fragments passed back and forth between the bassoon and piano, which develops into a canon-like texture with rhythmic dissonance of different note groupings of the technical passages occurring simultaneously such as quintuplet, sextuplet and septuplet. Eventually, a more melodic line emerges from the chaos in the bassoon part, which the piano begins to echo. A return to the previous texture takes over again. Later, new material emerges consisting of a disjunct large interval nonuplet with rests inserted into the phrase that occurs in the piano underneath glissandos that becomes a melodic line in the bassoon. The piano switches between textures of the disjunct line and echo the bassoon creating quick character changes. Eventually, this is interrupted by the technical canon-like chaotic section returning again. It develops into new material of thirty second notes overtop of accompaniment figures, whose roles alternate between the bassoon and piano each phrase. This leads into a large and virtuosic bassoon cadenza featuring technical flourishes, large intervals, and extended techniques. A return to the opening material occurs to conclude the work.

description: This work takes inspiration from Ukrainian folk music in a style that borrows melodic, ornamental, rhythmic, timbral and poetic elements fused with contemporary musical language and techniques. Pidgorna developed this style through her field work as a folklorist recording folk songs in Ukraine during 2012-2013. Lesya’s Song is based on an earlier work she wrote for two folk voices and layered double bass that features her own invented folk songs, which is set to poetry by nationalistic Ukrainian poet Lesya Ukrainka. The work takes inspiration from the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Musically, the invasion is represented by aggressive interruptions reminiscent of fanfares, which are going against the lyrical folk lines evoking imagery of singing amidst a war. An important motif throughout the piece is the frequent minor ninth leaps which encapsulate an attempt to capture voices breaking in lamentation. The piece contains three main sections. The opening “cantabile, with voice cracking” presents the repeated note motif in the English horn that depicts a singer’s voice softly cracking as they intensify a line. The bassoon immediately responds with a slurred minor ninth interval repeated twice to help establish a character of lament in the music. The English horn responds with a lyrical melody that begins with the minor ninth interval. These motifs continue to be developed and interact with one another throughout this section until we arrive at the second section “aggressive, bird-like, squawky.” In this section we begin a character change through the introduction of successive accented triplets that are reminiscent of a fanfare that destabilize the music creating the dichotomy of legato vocal-like melody and articulated disjunct characters. This depicts the juxtaposition of the imagery of singing amidst a war happening around them to the audience. The final section “rubato” returns back to the opening material and character. However, this time the score instructs to hold the rests a little longer creating a sense of longing for earlier times before the war began evoking the concepts of nostalgia and tradition. Overall, this piece takes elements of folk music and structures it in a contemporary manner to depict intense emotions.

description: This is a one-movement work that is centered around the idea of taking a fragment in a calmer character in a transparent texture that develops becoming more agitated and thicker texture. The work opens with short slurred virtuosic fragments leading to a longer note value played by the flute, which are responded to by large interval staccato passages that go from duple to triple note groupings in the winds. As the passage develops the parts slowly merge together creating a new and more chaotic texture. Eventually, this section winds down ending with a texture of a repeated note changing rhythmic patterns from duple, sextuplet, and nonuplet in the harp combined with inhaling and exhaling noises in the flute. The next main section “Lento” combines the virtuosic fragments from the opening now in homorhythm creating a calmer character overtop of prepared effects in the harp and piano. As it develops the winds become more contrapuntal and add extended techniques such as glissando to explore a variety of textures and timbres in the ensemble. Next, an A tempo occurs that consists of a constant line of thirty-second notes passed around the ensemble overtop of multiphonic notes creating a thick and busy texture. Eventually, the ensemble switches to the large interval motif from the opening, while the piano continues the thirty-second note texture combining elements from earlier into this continual texture. The final section “Rubato poco rallentando” combines all of the elements and motifs throughout to create one final climax of the parts all intertwining before rhythmically and motifically aligning together cohesively to unwind resulting in the harp and piano playing a final long note that the players wait for the sound to fully disappear to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work in three main sections. The first section opens with an ostinato of alternating eighth notes between the pitches “B♭'' and “C” in the left hand with isolated sixteenth note shots in the right hand. Eventually, the bassoon enters with rapid movement in which all the virtuoso possibilities of the modern bassoon are revealed. The second section is in a meditative character with a quiet singing quality through the long cantabile line in the bassoon overtop of the syncopated interjections of the piano. The final section is a stormy, concert finale that unites the main ideas of the first and second sections. It utilizes long rolled chords in the piano underneath the alternating eighth note motif from the opening now in the bassoon. However, this time the motif is very soft and staccato with rests interrupting the phrase to have the motif become shorter and more fragmented as each new statement appears until arriving at tied whole note Bb to conclude the piece.

description: This is a one-movement work with elements and motifs reminiscent of a Vivaldi bassoon concerto combined with neoclassical harmonic language and influence of liturgical music. The opening is a short twelve measure “Moderato” orchestral introduction presenting the main theme in a light and playful character through pizzicato. The bassoon then joins in over this texture with a slurred and dolce espressivo version of the theme. This leads into the next “Allegro” section that is a flurry of scalar sixteenth notes as an orchestral interlude. The third main section “Adagio religioso” the bassoon re-enters in the same legato character but much slower this time. The theme is overtop of a more chordal and legato string accompaniment that is arco. Then a return to “Moderato” occurs which mostly consists of long tones and a flourishing scale that goes into a tremolo motif in the strings, which the bassoon takes over. Then another return to the “Adagio religioso '' occurs as an orchestral interlude to return back to the opening “Moderato” legato theme with a contrapuntal string accompaniment. This leads to the next main section “Presto '' which features a fragment sixteenth melody that develops in a longer, more cohesive phrase in the bassoon overtop of the accompaniment of constant sixteenths in the strings. Eventually, once this section winds down we arrive at the final section “Lento”, which is a contrapuntal treatment of motifs from earlier in the work that elongates into long tones to conclude the piece.

description: This work is a four-movement suite in a neoclassical style with some elements of folklorism incorporated. The first movement “Humoresque” is in an ABA form in a vivace tempo with elements of folk music and dances. The A section has a light and playful character through a staccato eighth note melody with occasional slurred sixteenths in the first flute. This is overtop of accompaniment figures or homorhythmic passages. The B section is a legato character with a quarter note melody with an accompaniment consisting of a four-note ascending motif leading into a scale that gets traded around the ensemble. The second movement “Joke” is a quirky allegretto that alternates between articulated and slurred motifs to have constant character changes throughout. It features large, slurred intervals in the melody combined with a sigh-like motif consisting of a pickup into a quarter note slurred upward to an eighth note. The accompaniment often includes articulated large intervals in the bassoon and off beats or short syncopated motifs in the other instruments. The next movement “Waltz” incorporates stereotypical elements of Viennese waltzes in an andantino tempo. The accompaniment often has a downbeat quarter note or dotted half note to give the pulse and beats two and three in another voice underneath a legato and singing melody. The piece concludes with “A Fun Moment” which is an allegretto with folk elements that features a staccato bass line in the bassoon, accompaniment figures and a lively melody consisting of eighth and sixteenth notes.

description: This is a one-movement concerto that was inspired by the composer’s trip to Spain on a concert tour in 1994 written for his friend and bassoonist Taras Osadchiy. Therefore, the work features melodic and rhythmic motifs from Spanish folk music combined with elements of neoromanticism with virtuosity moments to bring a breath of fresh air to contemporary music. The work opens with a bassoon cadenza overtop of an ominous chord in the strings. The bassoon enters forte on a high C# in a declamatory manner introducing a couple of the work’s motifs such as the diminished fifth interval and three triplet eighth notes in an upper neighbour motion. This leads into an “Allegro” section where the bassoon alone presents the bass line ostinato based on a rhythmic motif of quarter note, dotted eighth rest, sixteenth note, and quarter note that provides an energetic dance-like character. The orchestra enters taking over the bass line ostinato while the bassoon introduces the fiery main theme that is centered around a string of triplets in upper neighbour motion. This section continues with the bassoon developing the theme while the orchestra plays the ostinato and other accompaniment figures. The next section consists of slurred arpeggiated eighth notes in the bassoon overtop of chords in the orchestra. This leads into a section where the bassoon plays the bass ostinato while the orchestra plays the melody before the bassoon takes over a variation of the theme overtop of accompaniment quarter notes in the orchestra. The next section continues this texture but with a lyrical melody consisting of long note values giving the bassoon the opportunity to showcase a contrasting character. This unwinds into an eighth note ostinato that morphs into the next section “Meno mosso” consisting of a vocal-like melody in the bassoon and a different eighth note ostinato overtop of chords in the orchestra. Finally, a return to an Allegro and virtuosic character occurs comprised of technical triplet passages both articulated and slurred showcasing the capabilities of the bassoon. Eventually, this connects into a rhythmically driven section where the bassoon and orchestra are in dialogue with syncopated fragments going back and forth between them. This develops in the technical climax of the concerto featuring weaving sixteenth note passages overtop of a bass line and off beats in the orchestra. Next, a return to the lyrical section occurs with a harp interlude to lead into a bassoon cadenza. This cadenza is a full display of the technical capabilities of the bassoon featuring double-tonguing and large intervals. Afterwards a return to the opening allegro section occurs. This is followed by an exciting, repeated note section in the bassoon displaying its ability for quick and crisp articulation. Afterwards, another return to the main theme occurs connecting into the final section “Vivo” as a coda featuring motifs from throughout the concerto to conclude the piece.

In 2014, during the Russian invasion of Ukraine, a town of the same name inspired by the film was established on an empty plot of land near Kyiv as a refuge for thousands of Jewish-Ukrainian people. description: This piece is composed of five short contrasting movements that provide a quick overview of a variety of characters a woodwind trio can achieve. However, none of the movements have been given any titles to denote the character. Overall, the piece is in a style reminiscent of French twentieth-century wind chamber writing similar in style to Eugène Bozza. The first movement is an allegro that has a sneaky character with writing that either has clear melody and accompaniment or unison amongst the members. The second movement is a typical vivace tempo movement with staccato eighths and slurred 16th motifs. The third movement is in a pastoral character with an often lazy feel from the quarter followed by an eighth motif throughout. The fourth movement is another allegro tempo that features trading sixteenths in the flute and clarinet that is combined with a very stereotypical bassoon accompaniment figure of staccato eighth notes in a big interval. As the piece continues the bassoon becomes more melodically involved and the roles in the ensemble switch. The final movement is a bright vivace featuring elements from throughout the piece combined with a repeated sixteenth motif.

description: This concerto is infused with the spirit of neoclassicism with each movement referencing a different musical period. The work reflects neoclassicism in both the style and orchestration choices, which is combined with elements of contemporary musical language. The first movement “Con moto” is reminiscent of the Baroque era, despite the pronounced sonata form that reminds one of a Concerto Grosso with its aspiration to rhythmic unity. Therefore, the bassoon is treated as one of the solo instruments within the dense sound of the orchestra. The second movement “Largo” evokes a direct association with Bach’s arias through the bassoon’s melodic line with an almost ascetic means of presenting the thematic material. In the reprise, the French horn solo enhances the spatial effect and serves as a preparation for the bassoon's virtuoso cadenza, which acts as a bridge between the second and third movements. The final movement “Allegro” has Mozartean inspiration through the thematic idioms and cadence that evoke a kaleidoscope of "recognition” with a highly anticipated quote from Mozart’s Symphony № 40, which leads back to the recapitulation. Finally, an elated coda brings back the expected elements for the end of a concerto while evoking parallels with Shostakovich's symphony finales.

description: This is a through-composed fantasy based on six songs by French singer Edith Piaf who sang in the cabaret and chanson genres. The six songs referenced are La vie en rose, Milord, Hymne a l’amour, La foule, Padam padam, and Non je ne regrette rien. The piece presents a variety of melodies and motifs from her songs that are developed in a variety of characters. The opening section “Calmo” begins with a chordal piano introduction leading into the violin presenting the first melody, which the bassoon joins with counterpoint during the violinist’s long notes. The next section “Scherzando” presents a staccato sixteenth note motif that develops over time until moving onto the third section “Piu tranquillo” that has a lazy quasi-jazz feel melody in the violin and bassoon overtop of piano accompaniment. Next, the piece goes into a stricter “Poco meno mosso” with a dialogue back and forth between the violin and bassoon over the piano’s waltz-like accompaniment. This is followed by two cadenzas, first in the violin and then the bassoon before returning to a tempo. Eventually, this ritardandos into a “Sostenuto” section that features an ostinato pattern in the piano, arpeggiation in the violin and a lyrical melody in the bassoon. description: This suite is originally written for a klezmer ensemble with it initially being adapted for the concert hall for violin and clarinet, and later for two bassoons or two clarinets. It includes five movements that elements of klezmer music and extended techniques such as frullato, glissando, and pitch bending to emulate this traditional style. The first movement “March” is a quick, articulated and energetic character where the two bassoons weave in and out of another overtop of a mostly chordal accompaniment piano part. The second movement “Nigun” is a traditional wordless song sung as a means of elevating the soul to God, which often has a solo line that is then repeated in unison and usually quite free in rhythm. In this movement, the first bassoon mostly plays a lyrical melodic line over an accompaniment piano part with the second bassoon joining into the first’s line throughout. The movement climaxes into a short middle tango section before returning to a short reprise of the melody before a first bassoon cadenza to arrive at a short coda to end it. The third movement “Grandmother’s Song” is an adagio that opens with the first bassoon playing a sentimental melody over chords in the piano. Eventually, the second bassoon enters as an echo of the first part type of response to represent a child singing along with their grandmother. The fourth movement “Jewish Tango” is an energetic dance that opens with the first bassoon playing a solo very typical klezmer type melody with rhythmic chords in the piano. Eventually, the second bassoon joins in harmony while playing rhythmic unison of the first. The rest of the movement continues in this fashion with the odd contrapuntal moment between the two parts. There is a small cadenza in the first part near the end. The final movement “Klezmer’s Polka” is in a similar style and structure of the previous movement, except the second bassoon has more independence of part with more contrapuntal writing throughout.

description: This is a three-movement work with text in old French from three poems by Charles d’Orleans for soprano. Charles d’Orleans was a medieval poet and the Duke of Orleans, who took over after his father’s assassination. On his mother’s deathbed Charles swore a traditional oath of vengeance for his father’s murder. Then after the French-English war he was imprisoned by the English for 24 years. It was during this period that the majority of his poetry was written. The first movement “Priez pour paix, dolce Vierge Marie” is in an andantino tempo is a prayer for peace where the speaker asks the Virgin Mary to bring them peace through the redemption of His blood to grant the end of war, which is ruining everything. Musically, it opens with a flute cadenza with rubato overtop of a cluster chord spaced in opening voicing in the piano. Then the piano introduces an ostinato figure of repeated triplet eighths and duple eighths marked “Chistko” (Evenly). The soprano then enters with the text and melodic content. This is in a dialogue with the flute and bassoon responding at the end of the first phrase. As it progresses the lines between the voice and winds become more interwoven and contrapuntal overtop of chords in the right hand of the piano and the ostinato in the left hand. This texture continues until the end of the movement. The second movement “La temps a laissie son manteau” in an andante tempo. The text is a poem in rondeau form using a repetition of the opening line throughout. It is about the transition from winter to spring and the beauty one encounters and experiences during this process. I believe this could be an analogy for the joy that will come when experiencing freedom from imprisonment and war. Musically, the melody in the voice begins on a repeated pitch “A” that opens up gradually becoming stepwise into larger intervals, mainly the perfect fourth and fifth. The ensemble plays an accompaniment role. The piano mostly plays sweeping arpeggiations leading to chords. Initially, the flute responds to the voice’s melody during rests that becomes a countermelody. The bassoon then enters to take it over, while the flute plays animato ascending trills on dotted quarter notes to create a more energetic and excited character to the music. The bassoon then shifts to an accompaniment role of dotted quarter and dotted half notes as it progresses allowing the flute to return to the countermelody role to conclude the movement.

description: This is a six-movement suite in a neoclassical style taking inspiration from Eastern European composers Bartok, Schnittke, Shostakovich, and Silvestrov. The work explores the concept of contrasts through articulation and line. The work is structured by beginning and ending with an unaccompanied solo with a series of duets in between them. The first movement “Tranquillo e espressivo” is a fantasy for solo flute. It begins with a lyrical and slurred melody and as the movement progresses becomes more virtuosic and technical featuring slurred sixteenth passages consisting of scalar and arpeggiated motion. This is contrasted with articulated triplet jumping around the range of the flute. The slurred passages become more disjointed overtime before ending in a sequential passage. Movements two through five are duets. The first one “Energico” features a weaving bass line that is slurred, which uses different one measure motifs as ostinatos. This is combined with a playful melody utilizing grace notes to get a whimsical character. In the opening the flute has the melody and the bassoon the bass line. Eventually, the roles reverse shortly with a lyrical melody in the bassoon before returning to original roles. This leads into a final adagio section in a contrapuntal texture. The next duet “Largo” has a quasi-improvisatory character with the two voices in a dialogue where one instrument plays eighth notes while the other is holding a long note value. Eventually, the voices come into unison playing a homorhythmic passage to bridge into a virtuosic thirty-second note section that weaves around each other. A contrasting section consisting of the flute playing a long note with a slow arpeggiated melody in the bassoon occurs. A return to the thirty-second note material occurs with variations to lead into a reprise of the opening material to conclude the movement. The next duet “Allegro moderato” has a humoresque character through a staccato eighth note line with large intervals in the bassoon underneath a chromatin melody in the flute. As the movement progresses the bassoon begins to fragment the melody in an echo while the flute has long notes developing into its own independent line creating a contrapuntal texture. The final duet “Lento” has an arpeggiated bass line and a vocal-like melody that switches between the two parts. The work concludes with an unaccompanied movement “Allegro marcato” in the bassoon, which is vigorous toccata in a quasi-ternary form. The A section is centered around repeated articulated sixteenth notes showcasing the bassoon’s ability to crisply articulate double-tonguing passages. The B section features slurred arpeggiated triplets that are sequentially exploring a variety of key centers. As the section develops sixteenth notes are introduced one beat at a time into the motif setting up a return to the A section character. However, the reprise of the A section is reduced and in different tonal centers than the opening.

description: This is a three-movement work in a neoclassical style using typical forms and structures combined with lots of exploration of key areas through tonicizations. The first movement “Sonata” is in an allegro moderato tempo opening with a section that features a theme in a march-like style in the clarinets in harmony overtop of a bass line in the bassoon and a countermelody in the flute. The next section presents a lyrical theme in the first clarinet that becomes more contrapuntal in the accompaniment as it develops. Eventually, the flute takes over with a weaving line of eighth notes that becomes fragmented passing around the ensemble. This gets transformed into an eighth, quarter, two eighth note motif that continues to pass around. This leads into an oscillating triplet quarter note ostinato in the second clarinet overtop of whole notes that connects into the opening material. The rest of the movement continues developing and bringing back material that shifts into different key areas briefly. The second movement “Intermezzo” is in an allegretto tempo has a lyrical melody that half is played by the flute and bassoon in harmony and the other half by the clarinets. Underneath are accompaniment figures when not playing the melody, such as a bass line on the second beat of each measure in the bassoon. The “Finale” movement is in ternary form in an allegro molto tempo which consists of a constant stream of eighth notes that is built on fragments being passed around the ensemble that as it progresses develops into a longer line. The movement continues in this manner through briefly touching a variety of key centers and accompaniment figures. The middle section unwinds to becoming mainly quarter notes in the melodic content.

The piano begins accompaniment and develops into a dialogue with the bassoon and eventually a more contrapuntal role with a countermelody. The final movement “Tarantella” is in ternary form featuring an A section with a stream of staccato eighth notes often in scalar motion in the bassoon overtop of accompaniment figures in the piano. The B section “Poco meno mosso” has a lyrical theme that alternates between triple and duple eighth notes in the bassoon overtop of chords in the piano.

description: This is a three-movement suite that uses folklore inspiration and elements of folk song and dance. The title takes inspiration from Trypillia, which was a culture from the neolithic and chalcolithic time period (5500-2750 BC) from the Carpathian Mountains, Dniester, and Dnipro regions of Ukraine discovered by archaeologist Vikenty Khvoyka in 1896.79 They are known for their pottery, agriculture, and their “burned house horizon.” This concept states that they burnt down their homes when an inhabitant passed away turning them from “dwellings of the living” into “homes of the dead” to make space for new ones.80 Therefore, the history of these people have been lost and forgotten as history has progressed.  The first movement “Morning in Trypillia” is an Andante moderato that alternates between two main sections. The first section features a folk-like melody of eighth and quarter notes that wanders around C mixolydian mainly in step-wise motion, perfect fifth and minor third interval. It is presented first by the flute alone followed by the whole ensemble playing it in unison. The occasional accompaniment figure occurs. The second section is a chorale texture comprised of half, quarter and eighth notes. As the section develops it switches tonality from C major to C minor and other various tonicizations in between. The next movement ”Light Over the Dnipro” is an Andante misterioso also has two main sections. It opens with the flute playing a solo one-measure ostinato in the lowest register. The clarinet then enters with a melody overtop that becomes a syncopated and rhythmic ostinato of tied eighth notes. Then bassoon and clarinet play a one-measure countermelody that becomes the rhythmic ostinato. Eventually, the oboe enters with a melody of half and dotted half notes overtop of the two ostinatos that are intertwined. The second section ”Piu mosso” is livelier with a dance-like character in a triplet meter that has a homorhythmic texture of eighth and quarter notes. As it develops it becomes fragmented and passes around the ensemble, which then gets interrupted with two-measures of the opening flute ostinato before returning to the homorhythmic texture. The movement concludes in a similar manner with the flute ostinato dying away. The final movement ”Dance of Ancestors” is an energetic dance that opens with a rhythmic ostinato of eighth followed by a quarter note in an perfect fifth interval in the clarinet and bassoon. The flute plays a virtuosic sixteenth and eighth note melody with grace notes. Next, the oboe enters with a dotted quarter note counter-melody. Eventually, the oboe, clarinet, and bassoon play a passage of sixteenth notes underneath the flute melody. The section continues with the melody passing around the ensemble while switching accompaniment textures underneath. The second section presents new melodic material that rotates around the ensemble. The movement continues to alternate between the material to conclude the work.

description: The first movement “Allegro” opens with multiphonics passing between each of the soloists, while the orchestra interweaves sixteenth note triplets in a chromatic motion creating a chaotic and unsettled atmosphere. Eventually, the texture settles into a syncopated homorhythmic passage of short fragments by the soloists, while the orchestra creates a dialogue of the chromatic motif creating a pattern and order from the initial chaos. As it develops the orchestra becomes part of the dialogue with the soloists, which allows for the fragmented statements to become a longer phrase creating cohesion in the whole ensemble. This gets interrupted by a return of the triplet motif but with more repeated and scalar motion inserted creating a sense of momentum to the phrase. This is in a dialogue texture as it rotates around the soloists. As it develops the texture becomes more contrapuntal allowing it to dive back into chaos. Eventually, the soloists introduced a new motif played in homorhythm based around the augmented fourth interval almost imitating a siren as an attempt to regain control. The movement continues in this manner between passages organized together and more disjunct and chaotic passages. This goes attacca into the second movement marked quarter note equals 45 beginning with a dissonant chorale-like passage in the soloists in dialogue with a bell in the percussion section. However, this soon breaks apart as each of the soloists plays different fragments of the opening in a contrapuntal texture as the orchestra slowly joins in and eventually taking over. Afterwards, the opening dissonant chorale returns but this time in a canon with the soloists being one group and the orchestra responding as another group two beats later. The movement continues alternating between the chorale and fragmented sections with a flute cadenza before the final section of the movement, which reverses the order with the soloists responding to the orchestra. The final movement marked quarter note equals 100 begins with material reminiscient of the first movement. This time we have ostinato sixteenth notes, which the pattern changes with each successive passage combined with a syncopated rhythmic melodic line. However, this time the rhythmic line continues developing and growing rather than small repetitive motifs. As it progresses motifs from earlier in the work such as the weaving chromatic triplet sixteenth and augmented fourth (now written as diminished fifth) are snuck into the texture creating a cohesive synthesis of the work. The movement continues playing with the already established motifs while presenting new materials and textures that often get reworked into material that is familiar, such as the opening sixteenths becoming more chromatic, which creates a merging of the old and new. Eventually, the soloists vocally sing “jazz licks” which essentially are the various rhythmic motifs from earlier being combined to create a rhythmic interplay imitating improvised jazz scatting. This results in only the soloists singing and the orchestra snapping their fingers on the final beat to conclude the work.

description: Na Tr’okh (For Three) is a post-Soviet phrase for when men get together to drink horilka (vodka). The work is structured to imitate a casual conversation that ebbs and flows like men chatting at a bar together. The piece opens with three distinct characters between the three parts, which could represent different roles within the conversation. The oboe has a longer, lyrical line reminiscent of one man telling a story while the bassoon has a short staccato line that interjects similar to a man interrupting and responding throughout the story. Finally, the clarinet produces air noises representing a role of a man actively listening along to the exchange. The piece develops into a fiery, technical section where each instrument passes the line around, like when a conversation gets heated with different opinions. This also includes the introduction of extended techniques such as frullato and multiphonics to help convey a more agitated character. Finally, after the piece climaxes the three instruments play a short unison passage to signify that they found a common ground and agreement leading into a slower more dialogue-like section that utilizes quarter-tones to create an expressive quality imitating the inflections fluctuations that naturally occur in speech. Finally, the piece ends with a slap tongue and playing with no reed section to create a whimsical, drunk character leading to the three musicians slumping over asleep in their chairs.

description: These three pieces are from a cycle of five works (two additional unaccompanied works) written for bassoon titled The Bassoonist’s Notebook. It was written throughout Runchak’s studies as a student at NMAU, which is dedicated and premiered by his classmate Taras Osadchiy. This is a three-movement work centered around the concept of contrasting characters throughout. The first movement “Improvvisazione” features a semitone motif based around D flat that develops through dialogue between the piano and bassoon, which later returns throughout the other movements. The work begins with a hyperchromatic piano introduction, presenting a solo chromatic line with minimal motion that gradually carves out motific space by expanding the material to reach an arrival. This arrival at the minor third interval of the pitches “E♭” to “C” becomes an important interval that Runchak uses to tie structural elements throughout the work together, such as to interrupt the rhythmic motif consisting of sixteenth, dotted sixteenth thirty second and tied sixteenths that is being established in the first movement. The movement continues in this dialogue that allows the motif to expand further outwards eventually resulting in the bassoon playing a glissando to the highest possible note they can play. The following movement “Burlesca” is a fast, articulated movement that resembles a dance that gets thrown off constantly by the changing metrical emphasis from the constantly changing meters. This movement is constantly switching between rhythmic motifs of two versus three eighth notes in the bassoon achieved through alternation between 6/8 and 5/8 metres. However, an ambiguity is inserted into the phrasing with the piano’s right hand playing five equal eighth notes slurred together in one connected line that blurs the emphasis of the larger alternating beats. This intentional ambiguity and playing with time continues developing as it becomes a line of quarter notes (or tied eighth notes) in the piano’s right hand and a syncopated line in the left hand. Throughout this movement the development of the sections is achieved through an increasing and organized chaos by having the phrases begin as small fragments, often in a homorhythmic and monophonic texture, but slowly introduces elements to the phrase that adds up over time until it has nowhere further to go and climaxes suddenly at the moment of peak chaos allowing for a restart of the material or introduction of new material. The final movement “Dialogo” features slow monologue-like phrases based on a dotted eighth and sixteenth note rhythmic motif alternating between the bassoon and piano. The movement opens with a cantabile line based around the motif from the opening of the work that expands outwards in the solo bassoon. The piano then provides a brief interlude of new material allowing the bassoon to attempt the opening material again. The movement continues in this manner until the piano concludes with their final interlude dying away.

description: The title Vyshyvanka is a Ukrainian word for the traditional embroidered shirts that are worn in Ukraine and the diaspora, which are a proud symbol of culture and identity. I believe the piece is centered around finding a balance between folkloric and avant-garde elements to represent the modern identity of Ukrainians, who are trying to balance the traditional elements of their identity with the complexities of the modern day. The piece opens with a folk like motif that is traded between a solo accordion and solo bassoon. This is then taken over by the oboe and clarinet, with the accordion providing an accompaniment role. However, this accompaniment begins to blur the lines through cluster chords that begin the introduction of atonality and avant-garde stylistic characteristics. This blurring of the texture leads into an unbalanced dance-like section in 5/4 through short staccato passages interacting amongst the ensemble. However, this gets interrupted by the accordion blurring the lines with a weaving chromatic line bringing back the cluster chords and avant-garde elements. The section develops and expands until climaxing into another unbalanced dance-like section for the rest of the piece. The dance is constantly shifting meter and utilizing contemporary techniques such as frullato and multiphonics to juxtapose the two aspects of identity.

description: This piece is three movements inspired by the Greek painter El Greco from the Renaissance era. He is known for his dramatic and expressionistic style that featured elongated figures and phantasmagorical images that married Byzantine traditions with Western painting. The first movement “Tempo sostenuto” has a mysterious character featuring prepared piano creating an eerie effect while the bassoons playing legato phrases in their lowest registers. As the movement progresses the movement intensifies to a faster agitated character depicting what the listener initially perceived was not exactly as it appeared on first glance, common in El Greco’s painting. The second movement “Tempo ad libitum, eccitando” is a much more exciting character with the rhythmic energy being a key feature as majority of the movement has constant eighth notes occurring. This movement is structured around the dialogue and passing of these eighth notes throughout the ensemble. The third movement “Tempo ad libitum, drammatico” is a very energetic and passionate character. The movement opens with sforzando prepared piano motifs responding to dramatic short fragments in the bassoons. This evolves into busy aleatoric accompaniments under short fragments in a call and response texture in the bassoons. This section ends abruptly to allow for the contrasting ”sostenuto, religious” ending section to be an effective surprise that features long tones moving in canon reminiscent of renaissance music in a modern re-interpretation.

description: This is a four-movement suite that utilizes elements of classical music combined with inspiration from Ukrainian folk music and dance. The first movement “Allegro con moto” opens with chords that weave between consonant and dissonant in the ensemble. The flute then presents the first theme for the introduction based around augmented chords which the oboe joins in a contrapuntal manner while the flute develops the theme. Eventually, the chords in the ensemble become a syncopated ostinato of eighths and sixteenths and a bass line underneath. Next, a cantabile main theme is presented in the flute that throughout the movement undergoes different textures provided by the accompaniment. This is interrupted every so often by a diminished chord forte-piano chord on repeated eighth notes in the ensemble that grows for two measures before returning back to the main theme material. The next movement “Pastorale” features a semplice melody consisting of eighth, quarter, and dotted quarter notes. It is first presented consonant in thirds by the flute and oboe overtop of a major chord drone in the clarinet, bassoon and horn. As the movement progresses the melody passes around the ensemble becoming more virtuosic, while harmonic shifts to more dissonance and folk harmonies such as using the Ukrainian minor scale, while the accompaniment parts become more intricate and contrapuntal. The third movement “Andante” is an arrangement of the Ukrainian folk song “Nich yaka misyachna” (What a Moonlit Evening) that is first presented as a clarinet solo of the melody overtop of a bass line of longer note values in the bassoon. Throughout the movement it undergoes variations such as a chorale section of the melody in homorhythm and a fugal-like section. The final movement “Scherzo and Ukrainian Dance” is in ternary form in an energetic and lively character. The A section is a scherzo that has virtuosic sixteenth note passages that pass around the ensemble overtop of accompaniment figures such as trading eighth notes between pairs of instruments such as the bassoon and clarinet, a three scalar sixteenth notes leading to three repeated eighth notes motif in the flute, and vocal-like melody of eigth, quarter and half notes in pair of instruments such as the horn and bassoon. The B section is a Hopak featuring a bass line in the bassoon, off-beats in the horn, and a melody in the oboe, which the flute joins in on the second phrase of each section exploring a different harmony each time. Eventually, the clarinet enters with a virtuosic line that utilizes glissandos and vibrato that takes over leading into a cadenza to set up a return to the scherzo A section to conclude the work.

description: This is a six-movement suite that utilizes elements from Hutsul folk songs and dances often using Eastern European scales and tonalities. This work demonstrates Shamo’s ability to write music rich in melody that decorate Ukrainian national musical motifs through its diverse breadth of emotions evoked. The first movement “At the meadow” (Na polonnyni) is in an intrada ad libitum tempo that begins with a bassoon solo in an improvisatory manner, which the other winds respond in dialogue during its long notes. The rest of the movement takes this theme and motifs and develops them alternating between contrapuntal and homorhythmic textures. Eventually, a return to the opening material occurs in the same texture. The second movement “Chabarashky” is an energetic folk dance in an allegro moderato tempo consisting of a fiery melody of eighth and sixteenth notes, syncopated accompaniment figures, and a staccato eighth note bass line with large intervals. Throughout the movement the material develops into tutti passages of staccato sixteenth notes. The next movement “Spivanochky” in an andantino pastorale tempo featuring a cantabile folk-like melody, eighth note arpeggiated ostinato, and chords. As the movement develops a countermelody is added into the texture. The fourth movement “Hahilka” in a moderato leggiero tempo that alternates between two sections 1) a descending staccato eighth note line in cannon leading to trill tied to a virtuosic septuplet in canon, and 2) an ominous folk melody played in harmony overtop of an ostinato. Slight variations occur as the material returns throughout. The following movement “Mountain Stream” (Hirskyi Potik) is in an allegro tempo centered around weaving sixteenth note passages imitating a running stream of water. A sequential eighth note motif interrupts it throughout leading to sixteenth notes being passed around the ensemble before returning to the original weaving line. A folk-like melody is introduced overtop of this texture. The final movement “Hutsulka” is another fiery folk dance in an allegro tempo featuring a syncopated staccato bass line, rhythmic driving repeated staccato eighth notes, and a virtuosic melody consisting of eighth and sixteenth notes with grace notes. Variations to the accompaniment and texture occur throughout such as passages of sixteenth notes in the accompaniment either a single line or passing around.

description: This piece is inspired by the idea of an actor reciting a monologue on stage. The structure of the piece resembles a speech going through a variety of characters creating a wide range of moods from mediation to agitation. The first section is centered around the pitch E-natural and utilizes inspiration from sonorism. The piece opens with a long note that in a free and calm character explores the various manipulation of timbre possible on the bassoon through, vibrato, quartertones, different timbral fingerings, glissando and smorzato to create slight variations like an actor beginning a start of a speech with a small idea that is growing and developing. The piece slowly opens up pitch wise leading into the next section that is a coherent melodic idea, like an actor expanding the speech into a main idea through the formulation of complete sentences. As this section develops the music becomes much more rhythmic, the character of the piece becomes more frantic and passionate, almost creating a dialogue amongst oneself how an actor would defend their points and position in the middle of a monologue. The piece eventually slows down reverting back to the opening character but with a full musical language incorporated, as if an actor coming to a conclusion. Stylistically, the piece combines elements of modality with free atonal techniques. An example of this is the use of the chromatic scale commonly used in classical music, but extending its tonality to include quarter tone pitches not common in classical playing and bassoon technique.
