description: This quintet is written in a postmodernist style that combines elements from various eras with contemporary languages such as atonality. The first movement “Andante” opens with an offstage horn playing a fanfare type motif typical of the past. The upper winds respond creating a call and response dialogue allowing the horn motif to develop with each successive phrase. Eventually this leads to the bassoon taking over the soloistic role from the horn allowing all the instruments to re-enter beginning to combine their parts together. This leads to a frantic trill section where the horn enters on stage and finally merges their lines together into a cohesive ensemble. The second movement “Fuga” opens with an unmetered dialogue between the upper winds. The next section is a juxtaposition of lyrical line in the bassoon and horn with a quick and staccato line in the upper winds. This concept is contrasted and alternates with aleatoric sections to explore the different possibilities of time within ensemble playing. The third movement “Andante” opens with the clarinet, bassoon and horn each having a soft, independent line that weaves in and out of each other with occasional moments of clarity when the parts line up together. This concept then continues in a duo with the flute and oboe which eventually becomes combined together. Eventually, a solo line in the oboe emerges from this thick texture with the other instruments dropping out. This allows them to re-enter independently one at a time with a new fugal type texture, which develops and expands until we get a more traditional chorale type texture typical of an Andante movement. This leads into the final section which features some elements of earlier like the weaving lines with new material such as fast fragments and short staccato passages. The final movement “Allegro moderato” explores the concept of pulse and time . The opening of the movement has the bassoon and horn still playing in the previous movement’s tempo while the others begin a typical fast and spirited finale movement. This idea continues throughout by having different tempos simultaneously occurring. Eventually, the ensemble solidifies their tempo together leading the final section of the piece. The very end of the piece returns to a variation of the fanfare that opened the piece, which involves the other instruments improvising as they go off stage leaving the horn separated from the ensemble once again.

This is a three-movement work in a neoclassical style using typical forms. The first movement “Allegro ma non troppo” is in ternary form and begins with a dialogue between two groups in the ensemble. The flute and bassoon have a lyrical and slurred line while the oboe, clarinet, and horn have a staccato eighth note line. As it develops the staccato line becomes syncopated. This material develops into a contrapuntal texture with some of the lines utilizing fragmentation from the earlier material and others presenting new material. The fragmentation is often passing around in a dialogue. The movement continues bringing back the themes in different textures and combinations. The next section “Lento assai” is a lyrical flute solo consisting of eighth notes leading to longer note values overtop of accompaniment figures. The return to the A section features new fragmentation and combination of the material. It also presents the Lento assai theme and fragments now in this more energetic character. The following movement “Adagio” has an espressivo line in a semplice character first in unison in unison in the clarinet and bassoon that continues in a canon-like texture as it develops to be more active with eighth notes incorporated in. The final movement “Rondino” has a form of ABACADA. The A section begins with a three eighth note motif in the bassoon consisting of the pitch “C” going up an octave than back down an octave to a “Bb” unexpectedly. The flute and clarinet start with fragments that get expanded into a playful theme of eighth notes with various syncopations from rests. As the movement progresses the bassoon line becomes virtuosic passages of sixteenth notes outlining the harmonic progressions. The B section “Andante” is an espressivo and lyrical solo in the oboe with no accompaniment. The return of the A begins with the bassoon ostinato but with a variation to the theme in the horn and a new line added in the upper winds. The C section “Subito meno mosso, cantabile” presents material reminiscent of the second movement. The next return of the A section is all variated material. The D section “Andante” is an espressivo and lyrical line that passes around the ensemble with short virtuosic fragments, which develop into contrapuntal lines. The final return to the A section features the bassoon ostinato in a different tonal area with a a couple co lines of earlier material combined together.

instrumentation: fl, ob, cl, bsn, hn, pno
premiere: 2015 in Kyiv by Ensemble Nostri Temporis
description: This is a one-movement work inspired by surconventionalism utilizing one convention or algorhythm throughout. Surconventionalism is centered around the idea of polystylistic music by composing music based on existing musical structures placed in a different context in order to create a new reality. Therefore, conventional language is used by the composer while also consciously breaking the rules governing its syntax by the unexpected and untypical juxtaposition of traditional elements to distort the listener’s expectations. This results in the transformation of the basic structure of music to achieve a deep structure through distortion techniques. Fox opens with a quarter note melody in the lowest register of the piano that is based on a two-note chromatic sequence. This line continues for the entire piece with small transformations over time. This is combined with a long tone motif in the winds where each voice enters in a cannon. This motif evolves over time becoming more active until it becomes a fragmentation of the piano line. Later the horn contrasts this with a different fragmentation briefly. Eventually, the long note motif becomes its own melodic line through all of the staggered entries in close succession of each phrase. At the end of the piece the winds join into a transformed version of the melody for three measures leading to a whole note in the clarinet overtop of the quarter notes in the piano. This texture dies away into silence to conclude the piece.

key: I (G major) II (G minor) III (G major) IV (A minor) V (none) VI (D major) VII (G major)
description: This is a six-movement suite in a folklorism style utilizing elements of folk melody and dance depicting the life in the past of an average village person. The first movement “Departure of a country carriage” is in ternary form using a Da capo al fine. The A section “Allegretto” is in a homorhythmic texture featuring a syncopated melody through the use of ties comprised of quarter and eighth notes. The B section “meno mosso” features an arpeggiated motif in the horn and clarinet that leads to a drone, which the flute and oboe play a short melody overtop of. The next movement “The beauty of road landscapes” is in an an “Allegro ma non troppo” tempo and has two main sections that alternate: 1) a sixteenth note line in the flute overtop of syncopated eighth note accompaniment figures and 2) a homorhythmic section comprised of a two-measure motif made up of eighth, sixteenth, and a dotted eighth notes. As the first section returns the accompaniment undergoes slight variations. The third movement “Breakfast on the grass under a canopy of trees” is in an “Andante” tempo and has a ternary form fully written out. The A section consists of a melody in thirds in the oboe and bassoon combined with an accompaniment line in the clarinet and horn. The B section marked “Trio” is a contrapuntal texture between the flute, oboe, and clarinet. The following movement “The playful games of children around a hazel bush” is in an “Allegretto” tempo consists of a melody and an accompaniment line that passes around the ensemble in different groupings that eventually results in the ensemble playing all together. The fifth movement “A conversation of shepherds’ pipes” is marked “Rubato” consisting of short virtuosic fragments passing between the flute, oboe and clarinet overtop of long tones. The bassoon and horn are tacet this movement. The subsequent movement “Meeting with an old barrel organist” is in an “Andantino” tempo that opens with an arpeggiated eighth note ostinato motif in the horn. The oboe enters with a melody and the flute, clarinet, and bassoon play chords. The final movement “Dances at sunset and walking by the lake” is very similar to the first movement. It has the same A section, but has a new B section in a moderato tempo. It features chords in the oboe, horn and bassoon underneath a melody in the flute and clarinet.

premiere: in summer 2025
description: The title “Shumka” is a Ukrainian word meaning “whirlwind” which is represented through the spinning sixteenth note motifs that constantly get passed around the ensemble at a fast and virtuosic pace combined with unexpected dissonances. The work is in a ternary form. It opens with the flute presenting the main theme that whirls around the middle register of the instrument in a scalar and sequential manner. This theme then gets fragmented as the other instruments enter in a polyphonic texture playing fragments from the theme. This leads to a long note in the flute overtop of an oscillating passage of minor second sixteenths in the oboe. As the section develops the fragments become longer and more intricate creating full independent lines. Throughout the A section the oscillating minor second motif is used for structural purposes to separate the smaller sections within the A section and has more instruments joining in with each successive reiteration. The B section features longer note values that weave between consonant and dissonant harmonies combined with dynamic hairpins emulating wind or a storm whirling around. The section develops by undergoing rhythmic diminution that allows for shorter note values to be introduced into the texture. This texture morphs the material into the return of the A material. In the return new tonal areas are tonicized throughout before returning to the home area of “G” allowing the work to end with a G major chord.

key: I (G major), II (C minor), III (A minor), IV (A minor)
description: This is a four-movement suite inspired by the animated film The Tale of Despeareaux, that follows the adventures of a mouse named Despeareaux in France who is sent to the dungeons for violating their laws by talking to humans. The first movement “Allegro” is an energetic and bright character. The opening begins with a lyrical melody in rhythmic unison that becomes more contrapuntal and staccato as the phrase progresses until the instruments have independent lines, like the beginning of a story slowly unfolding and sharing more details. The movement ends by the melody being interrupted with unexpected half note trills leading to a “mysteriously” section that ambiguous weaves around harmonically and ends without a cadence creating anticipation for the next movement. The second movement “Allegretto” is a humoresque and ironic eighth note accompaniment in the bassoon with an oboe melody that has an unsettled and unstable character due to the unexpected rests and accents thrown in. As the movement progresses the bassoon joins in as a countermelody with sixteenth notes. The third movement “Largo” has an ominous character through the use of dissonance added into the harmonic progressions. The form is ABA with the A section being a slow contrapuntal dialogue that leads to a rhythmic unison string of eight notes that create unexpected intervals and dissonances often on the offbeats. The B section is singing oboe melody overtop of an arpeggiated bass line in the bassoon. The final movement “Allegro” is an energetic dance-like character that often has an air of mysterioso to it due to the unexpected harmonies that appear. Often the bassoon has a bass line or a countermelody underneath a melody in the oboe. The movement features lots of sudden character achieved through the contrasting staccato and legato markings throughout.
